passport.market: One major pair (EUR/USD or GBP/USD), H4 for direction, H1 for timing, traded during the London or London–New York overlap.
passport.wait_for: A clear trend on H4 (higher highs and higher lows, or lower highs and lower lows) and price pulling back into a marked support or resistance zone that lines up with that trend.
passport.trigger: A closed H1 rejection candle out of the zone in the trend direction — buy above its high for longs, sell below its low for shorts — with a stop or limit order, never a chase.
passport.stop: Beyond the zone and the trigger candle's wick, plus the spread. Position size calculated so the stop costs no more than 0.5–1% of the account.
passport.target: The next opposing swing or zone, and at least 2R away. If the next obstacle is closer than 2R, there is no trade.
passport.avoid: Ranges with no clear swings, the 30 minutes either side of high-impact news, spreads wider than 20% of the stop, more than one open trade, and any trade you cannot size before you click.

lessons.title: What Forex Is, and Who Is on the Other Side of Your Trade
lessons.summary: Explain in plain English what the foreign exchange market is, why currency prices move, who trades it, and where a retail trader actually fits.
lessons.html:
Every time someone changes pounds into euros for a holiday, a business in Leeds pays an invoice in dollars, or a pension fund in Tokyo buys American bonds, a currency is sold and another is bought. Add up every one of those exchanges across the world and you get the foreign exchange market — forex, or FX. It is the largest financial market on earth by a wide margin, trading several trillion dollars' worth of currency every day.

That size is the first thing beginners hear, usually followed by something about opportunity. We would rather start somewhere more useful: what you are actually doing when you "trade forex", who you are doing it with, and why the price moves at all. Get these three things straight and the rest of this course — pips, lots, leverage, charts, risk — will slot into place instead of floating around as jargon.

This course is free and every lesson is unlocked. It is also, deliberately, not a strategy course. It is the foundation every strategy sits on. Traders who skip it tend to pay for it later, in money rather than time.

Trading forex means trading one currency against another

You cannot buy "the dollar" on its own in the forex market. A currency only has a price in terms of another currency. So everything in forex is quoted as a pair: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY and so on.

The quote EUR/USD 1.0850 means one euro costs 1.0850 US dollars. If that number rises to 1.0950, a euro now buys more dollars than it did — the euro has strengthened against the dollar, or, saying the same thing the other way round, the dollar has weakened against the euro. If it falls to 1.0750, the euro has weakened.

That is all a forex chart shows: the changing exchange rate between two currencies. When you trade it, you are taking a view on which of the two will strengthen relative to the other.

Here is the part that trips people up. The same economic story can make one chart go up and another go down, depending on which currency is written first.

KEY POINT

A forex price is an exchange rate. A rising chart means the first currency is strengthening against the second; a falling chart means it is weakening.

Why exchange rates move

Currencies are priced by supply and demand like anything else. Demand for a currency rises when people need more of it: to buy that country's goods, invest in its companies, or hold its bonds. Some of the biggest, most persistent drivers are:

  • Interest rates. Money tends to flow towards currencies that pay a higher return for holding them. When a central bank such as the Bank of England, the European Central Bank or the US Federal Reserve raises or cuts rates — or even hints that it might — its currency often moves sharply.
  • Economic data. Employment, inflation and growth figures change expectations about future interest rates, so they move currencies too. The monthly US jobs report is a famous example.
  • Trade and capital flows. A country that exports heavily, or attracts lots of foreign investment, sees steady demand for its currency.
  • Risk appetite. In nervous markets, money often moves towards currencies seen as safe places to park it; in confident markets, it flows back out.

You do not need to forecast any of this to trade, and this course does not ask you to. But you do need to know that these events exist, because they are the moments when prices jump, costs widen and beginners get hurt. We will mark them on charts throughout the course.

Who trades forex

There is no single forex exchange with a trading floor. Forex is an over-the-counter market: a global network of banks, brokers and electronic platforms dealing with each other directly. Roughly, the participants look like this.

Banks and dealers. The big international banks quote prices to each other and to their clients all day, and they handle the bulk of the volume. They are not, mostly, betting on direction. They make money from the gap between the price they buy at and the price they sell at, and from serving clients.

Businesses. Companies that buy or sell abroad convert currencies to pay bills and bring home revenue. Many also hedge — lock in exchange rates in advance — so that a currency move does not wreck their profit margins. Their trades are driven by business needs, not by charts.

Investment funds. Pension funds, asset managers and hedge funds move money between countries to buy shares and bonds, and some trade currencies directly as an investment. Their positions can be very large and held for months.

Central banks. They set interest rates and occasionally buy or sell their own currency directly. They are not trying to make a trading profit; they are trying to run an economy.

Retail traders. That is you. Individuals trading through an online broker, usually with small accounts relative to everyone above. Retail traders are a small slice of the total volume.

This matters for one practical reason: you are not the market's main character. Price will not wait for you, will not notice your stop, and does not owe you a trend. Your job is not to outsmart banks. It is to find situations where the odds lean slightly your way, risk a small and fixed amount on each, and survive long enough for that slight lean to matter. Most of this course is about the "small, fixed amount" and "survive" parts, because those are what beginners neglect.

COMMON MISTAKE

Believing that because the market is huge and open 24 hours, there is always a trade worth taking. Size and access are not the same as opportunity. Most of the time, the right decision is to do nothing.

How a retail trader actually trades

When you open an account with a retail broker and click "buy" on EUR/USD, you are not usually exchanging euros for dollars that land in a bank account. In most cases you are entering a contract whose value tracks the exchange rate. In the UK this is often a CFD (contract for difference) or a spread bet; elsewhere it is commonly a margin forex account. The details vary by country and broker, but the effect is the same: if the price moves your way, the contract gains value; if it moves against you, it loses value, and the gain or loss is settled in your account currency.

Three features of this set-up will come up again and again:

  1. You can profit from falling prices as easily as rising ones, by selling first. That is called going short, and it is covered in Lesson 4.
  2. You do not need the full value of the trade in your account. The broker lets you control a large position with a small deposit called margin. This is leverage, and it is the single most dangerous tool a beginner is given. Lesson 4 again.
  3. Every trade has a cost — at minimum the spread between the buying and selling price. Lesson 3 shows you how to measure it.

A word on regulators. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority regulates brokers offering these products, and you can check a firm's registration on its public register. Many other countries have equivalent bodies. A broker you cannot find on a proper regulator's register is a broker to walk away from. Regulators also require brokers to publish the percentage of retail accounts that lose money on these products, and those figures are consistently high. Read them. They are not there to scare you; they are there because they are true.

A practice drill before we start

Before we teach you anything else, here is a first look at the kind of judgement this course builds. You do not need any technical knowledge to answer it — only common sense about what you have just read.

Going deeper

How big is "big"? Industry surveys put global forex turnover at several trillion dollars a day, with the US dollar on one side of the large majority of trades. The practical consequences for you are liquidity and tight costs on the major pairs during busy hours — and the fact that no individual retail trader can move the price. Liquidity is not constant, though. It thins out in the gap between the New York close and the Asian open, around holidays and immediately before major news, and costs widen accordingly (Lessons 3 and 5).

Who is on the other side of your trade? With a retail broker, your trade's counterparty is usually the broker itself. Some brokers pass client orders on to banks and liquidity providers; others take the other side internally and manage the overall exposure. Neither model is automatically sinister — regulated brokers must treat client orders fairly and keep client money segregated — but it is worth understanding what your broker's model is and how it makes money (spread, commission, or both). Read the order execution policy. It is dull, and it is your money.

Rolling positions and swap. Because spot currency trades technically settle two days later, positions held past the daily roll-over time are charged or credited an overnight financing amount, called swap or rollover, based on the interest rate difference between the two currencies plus a broker charge. For short-term traders it is small; for positions held for weeks it becomes a real cost, and on some pairs it is charged in both directions. We cover it with the other costs in Lesson 3.

The honest picture. Retail forex is legal, regulated and accessible, and it is also a market where most retail accounts lose money. The main reasons are not mysterious: too much leverage, no fixed risk per trade, trading around news and in quiet hours, and treating each trade as a test of being right. Every one of those is fixable with knowledge and discipline, and that is what this course is for. Nothing here promises profit. What it can do is stop you losing money for avoidable reasons.

Summary

  • Forex is the global market for exchanging one currency for another, quoted in pairs such as EUR/USD.
  • A rising chart means the first currency is strengthening against the second; a falling chart means it is weakening.
  • Prices move on supply and demand, driven largely by interest rates, economic data, capital flows and risk appetite.
  • Banks, businesses, funds and central banks dominate volume; retail traders are a small slice and do not move the price.
  • Retail traders usually trade contracts that track the rate, with leverage and costs — both of which this course teaches you to control.

quiz.q: EUR/USD moves from 1.0800 to 1.0900. What has happened?
options: The euro has weakened against the dollar
The euro has strengthened against the dollar
The dollar has strengthened against the euro
quiz.why: One euro now buys $1.0900 instead of $1.0800, so the euro buys more dollars: it has strengthened. The dollar has weakened against it, which is the same fact seen from the other side.

quiz.q: The US dollar weakens against most currencies. Which pair of chart moves would you expect?
quiz.why: On EUR/USD the dollar is second, so a weaker dollar pushes the chart up. On USD/JPY the dollar is first, so a weaker dollar pushes the chart down. Always check which currency is written first.

quiz.q: Which of these is most likely to cause a sudden, large move in a currency?
options: A quiet afternoon with no news
A central bank interest rate decision that surprises the market
A retail trader placing a large order
The broker changing its chart colours
quiz.why: Interest rate expectations are one of the biggest drivers of currencies, so a surprise decision forces the whole market to reprice at once. A retail order, however large it feels, does not move a market of this size.

quiz.q: What does 'over-the-counter' mean in forex?
options: Trades happen only during bank opening hours
There is no single central exchange; participants deal through a network of banks, brokers and platforms
Only banks are allowed to trade
Prices are fixed once a day
quiz.why: Forex has no central exchange floor. It is a decentralised network, which is why it runs around the clock across time zones and why prices can differ very slightly between brokers.

quiz.q: In the drill chart, why was 'no trade' the right answer?
options: Because EUR/USD cannot be traded in the afternoon
Because the chart was going up
Because a major scheduled release was due, the morning had no direction, and costs and slippage are worst at that moment
Because the broker would have refused the order
quiz.why: There was no edge — just a flat morning — and the next candle was a news candle where price can swing violently both ways and costs widen. Choosing not to trade is a decision, and often the best one.

lessons.title: Currency Pairs, Pips and Lots — The Units of the Market
lessons.summary: Read any currency quote, measure any price move in pips, and convert pips into money for any lot size — in your own account currency.
lessons.html:
Imagine trying to follow a recipe where nobody agreed what a "cup" was. That is roughly the position of a beginner who opens a trading platform without knowing what a pip or a lot is. The numbers on the screen move, money goes up and down, and there is no way to connect the two.

This lesson fixes that. It introduces the three units everything else in forex is built on: the pair (what you are trading), the pip (how far price moved) and the lot (how much you traded). Once you can move between those three, you can answer the only question that really matters before a trade: if price goes this far against me, how much money do I lose?

There is some arithmetic here. It is all multiplication and division, and every example is worked in full. Take it slowly once; after that it becomes automatic.

Base and quote: reading a pair

Every pair has two currencies. The first is the base currency; the second is the quote currency. The price tells you how many units of the quote currency one unit of the base currency costs.

  • EUR/USD 1.0850 — one euro costs 1.0850 US dollars. Base EUR, quote USD.
  • GBP/USD 1.2700 — one pound costs 1.2700 dollars. Base GBP, quote USD.
  • USD/JPY 150.00 — one dollar costs 150 yen. Base USD, quote JPY.
  • EUR/GBP 0.8540 — one euro costs 0.8540 pounds. Base EUR, quote GBP.

When you buy a pair, you are buying the base currency and selling the quote currency. When you sell a pair, you are selling the base and buying the quote. So buying GBP/USD is a bet that the pound will strengthen against the dollar. Selling USD/JPY is a bet that the dollar will weaken against the yen.

Pairs fall into three rough groups:

  • Majors — the most traded pairs, all involving the US dollar: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD, NZD/USD. These have the most liquidity and usually the lowest costs. Beginners should start here.
  • Crosses — pairs of major currencies without the dollar, such as EUR/GBP, EUR/JPY or GBP/JPY. Perfectly tradeable, usually a little more expensive.
  • Exotics — a major currency against a smaller or emerging-market one, such as USD/TRY or EUR/ZAR. Wider spreads, sharper gaps, and more ways to get hurt. Not for this course.
KEY POINT

Buying a pair means buying the first currency and selling the second. The quote currency — the second one — is the currency your profit or loss is calculated in before conversion.

What a pip is

A pip is the standard unit for measuring a price move. For almost every pair it is the fourth decimal place: 0.0001. For pairs quoted in Japanese yen, where prices are around 100 or more, it is the second decimal place: 0.01.

So:

  • EUR/USD moving from 1.0850 to 1.0900 is a move of 0.0050, which is 50 pips.
  • GBP/USD falling from 1.2700 to 1.2665 is a move of 0.0035, which is 35 pips.
  • USD/JPY rising from 150.00 to 150.80 is a move of 0.80, which is 80 pips — because on yen pairs a pip is 0.01.

Most platforms show one more digit — EUR/USD 1.08503, for example. That fifth digit is a pipette, a tenth of a pip. Ignore it when counting pips, but do not be confused when you see it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Counting the pipette digit as a pip. On a five-digit platform, EUR/USD moving from 1.08500 to 1.08550 is 5 pips, not 50. If your sums ever give you a pip count ten times bigger or smaller than seems sensible, check the decimal place first.

What a lot is

A lot is the standard unit of trade size, measured in units of the base currency:

Size Units of base currency Platform shows
Standard lot 100,000 1.00
Mini lot 10,000 0.10
Micro lot 1,000 0.01

So buying 1.00 lot of EUR/USD means buying €100,000 worth of euros (against dollars). Buying 0.10 lots means €10,000. Buying 0.01 lots means €1,000. Most brokers allow sizes in steps of 0.01 lots, and some spread-betting accounts express size as money per point instead — the logic below is identical, only the label changes.

Do not let the big numbers alarm you. You do not need €100,000 in your account to trade a standard lot; leverage, covered in Lesson 4, lets you control it with a deposit. But the size of the position is what decides how much each pip is worth, and that is the number we care about.

Pip value: turning pips into money

Here is the one fact to memorise:

One pip on one standard lot is worth 10 units of the quote currency.

That follows directly from the definitions: 100,000 units × 0.0001 = 10. (For yen pairs: 100,000 × 0.01 = 1,000 yen — the same idea, because the pip is bigger.)

So, per standard lot:

  • EUR/USD and GBP/USD: $10 per pip (quote currency is USD).
  • EUR/GBP: £10 per pip (quote currency is GBP).
  • USD/JPY: ¥1,000 per pip (quote currency is JPY).

Mini lots are a tenth of that ($1 per pip on EUR/USD) and micro lots a hundredth ($0.10 per pip).

Now put pips and lots together. Profit or loss is simply:

Profit or loss = pips moved × pip value per lot × number of lots

A 40-pip move on EUR/USD is worth:

  • 1.00 lot: 40 × $10 × 1 = $400
  • 0.10 lots: 40 × $10 × 0.1 = $40
  • 0.01 lots: 40 × $10 × 0.01 = $4

Converting to your account currency

If your account is in the same currency as the quote currency, you are done. A dollar account trading EUR/USD makes and loses dollars at $10 per pip per lot.

Most readers of this course will have a pound account, though, and most popular pairs are quoted in dollars. So you convert. The rule: divide a dollar amount by the GBP/USD rate to turn it into pounds.

Worked example, all rates illustrative:

  • Account in GBP. Trading EUR/USD, 0.20 lots.
  • Pip value: $10 × 0.20 = $2 per pip.
  • GBP/USD is 1.2700, so $2 ÷ 1.27 = £1.57 per pip.
  • A 30-pip loss costs 30 × £1.57 = £47.24.

And on a cross quoted in pounds, there is nothing to convert:

  • Account in GBP. Trading EUR/GBP, 0.20 lots.
  • Pip value: £10 × 0.20 = £2 per pip.
  • A 30-pip loss costs £60.

For yen pairs, convert the yen amount into your account currency the same way. On USD/JPY at 150.00 with a dollar account, ¥1,000 per lot is ¥1,000 ÷ 150 = $6.67 per pip per lot. With a pound account, you would divide the yen amount by the GBP/JPY rate instead. Every platform shows pip values somewhere, and a good position size calculator does all this for you — but you must be able to check it by hand, or you will not notice when it is wrong.

Going deeper

Why pip value drifts. Pip value in your account currency depends on an exchange rate, so it changes slightly as rates move. On EUR/USD in a GBP account, £1.57 per pip at GBP/USD 1.2700 becomes about £1.53 if GBP/USD rises to 1.3100. For sizing a single trade, the current rate is fine. For anyone comparing trades across months, it is one more reason to measure results in R (risk units, Lesson 11) rather than in pounds.

Pips on gold, indices and other symbols. Many platforms list gold (XAU/USD), oil and stock indices alongside currencies. Their "pip" or "point" is defined by the broker, and it is not always the same between brokers. Gold, for example, is often quoted to two decimals with one pip defined as 0.10 — but check your platform's contract specification. Never assume a pip value outside the major currency pairs; look it up.

Contract specifications are the source of truth. Every broker publishes a specification for every symbol: contract size, minimum and step size, pip or point value, trading hours, and margin requirement. Five minutes reading it for the pair you trade will save you from the commonest error in retail trading — a position ten times bigger than intended because a pip or lot was misunderstood.

Spread bets. UK spread-betting accounts express size as "£ per point" instead of lots. If one point is one pip, then £1 per point on EUR/USD is equivalent to about 0.127 lots at GBP/USD 1.2700 (because 0.127 × $10 ÷ 1.27 ≈ £1). The arithmetic of risk is the same: points moved × money per point = profit or loss.

Summary

  • A pair is base/quote; buying it buys the base and sells the quote.
  • A pip is 0.0001 on most pairs and 0.01 on yen pairs; the fifth digit is a pipette.
  • A standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency; mini 0.10, micro 0.01.
  • One pip on one standard lot is worth 10 units of the quote currency; convert it into your account currency.
  • Profit or loss = pips × pip value per lot × lots. Know the loss at your stop before every trade.

quiz.q: GBP/USD falls from 1.2740 to 1.2695. How many pips is that?
quiz.why: 1.2740 − 1.2695 = 0.0045. On non-yen pairs a pip is 0.0001, so that is 45 pips.

quiz.q: USD/JPY rises from 149.20 to 149.65. How many pips?
quiz.why: 149.65 − 149.20 = 0.45. On yen pairs a pip is 0.01, so 0.45 is 45 pips.

quiz.q: You buy 0.30 lots of EUR/USD in a dollar account. What is each pip worth?
quiz.why: One standard lot is $10 per pip, so 0.30 lots is 0.30 × $10 = $3 per pip.

quiz.q: In a pound account, you trade 0.50 lots of EUR/GBP with a 24-pip stop. What does the stop cost if hit?
quiz.why: EUR/GBP is quoted in pounds, so one lot is £10 per pip and 0.50 lots is £5 per pip. 24 pips × £5 = £120. No conversion needed.

quiz.q: Buying EUR/USD means:
quiz.why: Buying a pair buys the base (first) currency and sells the quote (second) currency. You profit if the euro strengthens against the dollar.

quiz.q: In the 'Pound account, dollar pair' chart, why is the loss £47.24 rather than $60?
options: Because the broker charged a fee
Because $2 per pip was converted into pounds at the GBP/USD rate before multiplying by 30 pips
Because pound accounts get a discount
quiz.why: 0.20 lots on GBP/USD is $2 per pip; 30 pips is $60. Converted at 1.2700, $60 ÷ 1.27 ≈ £47.24. The pip count is the same; only the currency of the money differs.

lessons.title: Spreads and Costs — What Every Trade Really Costs You
lessons.summary: Read the bid and ask, measure a trade's full cost — spread, commission, swap and slippage — and judge whether that cost is small enough relative to your stop to be worth paying.
lessons.html:
Nobody runs a forex broker for fun. Every time you open and close a trade, you pay for the privilege. The fee is rarely presented as a bill; it is built into the prices you see, charged quietly per lot, or added overnight. Because it is quiet, beginners ignore it — and then wonder why a strategy that "should" break even keeps slowly bleeding.

This lesson makes the costs visible. You will learn where the spread comes from, how commission and swap work, why slippage exists, and — most usefully — how to judge whether a trade's cost is a rounding error or a serious handicap. That last judgement is about proportion, and it shapes which timeframes and stop sizes are realistic for you.

All prices and costs in this lesson are illustrative. They are in a realistic range for major pairs at a regulated retail broker, but yours will differ. Part of the job is measuring your own.

Two prices: the bid and the ask

At any moment, your platform shows two prices for each pair:

  • The bid — the price at which you can sell.
  • The ask (or offer) — the price at which you can buy.

The ask is always higher than the bid. The gap between them is the spread, measured in pips. If EUR/USD shows 1.08500 bid and 1.08512 ask, the spread is 0.00012, or 1.2 pips.

That gap is the dealer's margin. Think of the bureau de change at an airport: it buys your pounds at one rate and sells them back at a worse one, and the difference is how it pays the rent. A forex broker does the same thing, only with a far smaller gap.

A practical consequence: every trade starts slightly in the red. Buy at the ask, and if you closed immediately you would sell at the bid — 1.2 pips lower. Price has to move in your favour by at least the spread just to get back to zero.

Spread accounts and commission accounts

Brokers charge in one of two broad ways.

Spread-only (often called "standard") accounts. No separate fee; the broker's charge is built into a wider spread. On EUR/USD in busy hours you might see something like 0.8–1.5 pips.

Raw-spread or commission accounts. The spread is much tighter — perhaps 0.1–0.3 pips on EUR/USD in busy hours — but you pay a commission per lot. A common structure is around $7 per standard lot per round turn (opening and closing). On EUR/USD, where a pip on one lot is $10, $7 is 0.7 pips.

Add the parts to get your all-in round-trip cost:

  • Standard account: 1.2-pip spread + nothing = 1.2 pips.
  • Raw account: 0.2-pip spread + 0.7-pip commission = 0.9 pips.

The cheapest account type depends on how often and how large you trade, so compare them on this all-in number, not on the headline spread.

KEY POINT

Know your all-in cost per round trip, in pips, for the pair and the hours you actually trade. It is the entry fee for every trade, win or lose.

Spreads are not fixed

The spread changes all day. It is tightest when the most banks and dealers are active — the London session and the London–New York overlap — and widest when they are not:

  • Around the daily roll-over (around 22:00 UK time, depending on daylight saving), when liquidity is thin and dealers reset positions. Spreads can briefly widen to several times normal.
  • Before and during major news, when dealers pull back and prices jump.
  • On Monday's open and before weekends or holidays.
  • On less-traded pairs, all the time.

Swap: the overnight cost

If you hold a position past the daily roll-over, it is charged or credited swap (also called rollover or overnight financing). Swap is based on the difference between the interest rates of the two currencies, minus a broker charge, and it is applied for each night held. Many brokers apply three nights' worth on one weekday — commonly Wednesday — to cover the weekend.

Swap can be positive or negative depending on direction, but after the broker's charge it is often negative in both directions on some pairs. For a trade held a few hours, ignore it. For a trade held for weeks, it adds up. A position paying an illustrative −$7 per lot per night costs $210 per lot over thirty nights — the equivalent of 21 pips on EUR/USD. Your platform shows the current swap rates in each symbol's specification.

Slippage: the cost nobody quotes

Slippage is the difference between the price you asked for and the price you got. A market order fills at the best available price at the moment it reaches the market; if price is moving fast, that can be worse than the price you saw when you clicked. A stop-loss order, once triggered, also becomes a market order — so in a fast move it can fill beyond your stop level.

Slippage is usually small in calm, liquid conditions and can be large around news and opens. It can occasionally be in your favour. You only learn your typical slippage by logging the price you intended and the price you were filled at, on every trade.

The judgement that matters: cost as a share of your stop

A one-pip cost means nothing on its own. What matters is its size relative to your stop, because the stop is what you are risking.

  • 1.2-pip cost on a 40-pip stop = 3% of your risk. A rounding error.
  • 1.2-pip cost on a 10-pip stop = 12% of your risk. Noticeable.
  • 1.2-pip cost on a 5-pip stop = 24% of your risk. A heavy handicap, paid on every trade.

This is why the smallest timeframes, with the tightest stops, are the hardest place for a beginner to make the arithmetic work. A simple guard rail for this course: if your all-in cost is more than about a fifth of your stop, the trade is too expensive. Widen the stop (and reduce the size — Lesson 11), move to a higher timeframe, or skip it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Comparing brokers on the advertised "from 0.0 pips" spread. What matters is the all-in cost at the hours you trade, including commission and typical slippage. Measure it; do not trust the banner.

Going deeper

Measure, do not guess. For two weeks, at the times you intend to trade, note the spread on your chosen pair every 15 minutes, and log intended versus filled price on any demo orders. Take a bad-but-normal figure (around the 80th percentile, not the average) as your planning cost. Averages flatter you, because spreads are widest exactly when markets move.

Commission converts by pair. $7 per lot is 0.7 pips on EUR/USD and GBP/USD, where a pip on a lot is $10. On USD/JPY at 150.00, a pip on a lot is about $6.67, so $7 is about 1.05 pips. Convert before comparing.

Costs and the break-even win rate. If you risk S pips to make T pips and pay C pips per round trip, a winner nets T − C and a loser costs S + C. The win rate you need just to break even is (S + C) ÷ (S + T). With a 20-pip stop, 40-pip target and 1.2-pip cost: 21.2 ÷ 60 = 35.3%, against 33.3% with no costs. With a 5-pip stop and 10-pip target and the same cost: 6.2 ÷ 15 = 41.3%. Same reward-to-risk, same cost in pips — but the smaller trade needs eight more winners in every hundred just to stand still. These figures are arithmetic, not predictions of any strategy's results.

Guaranteed stops. Some brokers offer guaranteed stop-loss orders that cannot slip, for an extra fee charged when they are used. They can be worth it for trades held over weekends or through known events. Read the terms.

THE RULES
  • Know your all-in round-trip cost (spread + commission + typical slippage) in pips for your pair and hours
  • If the all-in cost is more than about a fifth of your stop, do not take the trade as planned
  • Avoid opening trades in the hour around the daily roll-over and immediately before major scheduled news
  • Check the swap rate before planning to hold a position for more than a few days

Summary

  • You buy at the ask and sell at the bid; the gap is the spread, and every trade starts behind by that amount.
  • Commission accounts swap a wider spread for a fee per lot; compare accounts on the all-in cost.
  • Spreads widen around the roll-over, news, opens and on thin pairs; slippage is worst at the same moments.
  • Swap is charged nightly on held positions and becomes significant over weeks.
  • Judge cost as a share of the stop: above roughly a fifth, the trade is too expensive.

quiz.q: EUR/USD is quoted 1.09210 bid / 1.09224 ask. What is the spread?
quiz.why: 1.09224 − 1.09210 = 0.00014. A pip is 0.0001, so that is 1.4 pips (the fifth digit is a pipette).

quiz.q: You want to buy GBP/USD. At which price will you be filled?
quiz.why: You buy at the ask, the higher of the two prices. You sell at the bid.

quiz.q: A raw account charges a 0.3-pip spread plus $7 per lot round turn on EUR/USD. What is the all-in cost in pips?
quiz.why: $7 on a $10-per-pip lot is 0.7 pips. Add the 0.3-pip spread: 1.0 pip per round trip.

quiz.q: Your all-in cost is 1.5 pips. Which stop size makes the cost a heavy handicap under this lesson's guard rail?
quiz.why: 1.5 ÷ 6 = 25% of the risk, above the one-fifth guard rail. On 15 pips it is 10%, on 30 pips 5%.

quiz.q: Why might a stop a few pips below price be hit around 22:00 UK time even if the chart barely moves?
options: Spreads can widen sharply at the roll-over, so the price you would sell at drops below your stop
Swap is deducted from the stop
quiz.why: A long position's stop triggers on the bid. When the spread widens, the bid can dip far enough to hit a nearby stop even without much real trading.

quiz.q: A trade is held for 20 nights at an illustrative swap of −$5 per lot per night, at 0.5 lots. What is the swap cost?
quiz.why: 20 nights × $5 per lot × 0.5 lots = $50. Swap scales with both time held and position size.

lessons.title: Long, Short, Leverage and Margin — and Why Leverage Is Dangerous
lessons.summary: Explain how buying and selling make money in either direction, calculate the margin a position uses, and measure how leverage turns small price moves into large account swings.
lessons.html:
Two features make retail forex very different from buying shares in an ISA. You can make or lose money as easily when prices fall as when they rise. And you can control a position many times larger than the money in your account. The first is genuinely useful. The second is the main reason beginners lose money quickly.

This lesson explains both properly: what going long and short actually means, what margin is, what leverage really does to the numbers, and what happens when an over-leveraged account runs out of room. The lesson ends with a rule that should stay with you for your whole trading life: your broker's leverage limit is not your risk limit. You decide risk with your stop and your position size. Leverage merely allows it.

All figures are illustrative and assume a pound account, a GBP/USD rate of 1.2700, and the 30:1 maximum leverage that UK and EU regulators currently allow retail clients on major pairs. Check your own broker's limits.

Going long and going short

Going long means buying a pair. You profit if it rises. Buy EUR/USD at 1.0850, sell it later at 1.0900, and you have made 50 pips.

Going short means selling a pair you do not already own, hoping to buy it back cheaper later. Sell EUR/USD at 1.0850, buy it back at 1.0800, and you have made 50 pips. Because a currency pair is always one currency against another, selling EUR/USD is simply buying dollars against euros. There is nothing exotic about it; it is just as normal as buying.

KEY POINT

Long profits from a rise, short profits from a fall. In both cases the stop sits on the side where you would be proven wrong.

What margin is

When you open a leveraged position, your broker does not lend you the full amount in a way you ever see. Instead, it sets aside part of your balance as a deposit to cover potential losses. That deposit is called margin.

With 30:1 maximum leverage, the margin required is 1/30 of the position's value, or about 3.33%.

Worked example:

  • You buy 0.50 lots of EUR/USD at 1.0850. That is €50,000.
  • In dollars: €50,000 × 1.0850 = $54,250.
  • In pounds: $54,250 ÷ 1.27 = about £42,717. That is the size of the position — its notional value.
  • Margin at 3.33%: £42,717 ÷ 30 = about £1,424.

So on a £2,000 account, a 0.50-lot trade "uses" £1,424 of margin and leaves about £576 of free margin — the room you have before the broker starts to worry. Margin is not a fee. It is returned when you close. But it limits how big a position you can open, and it sets the point at which the broker will close your trades for you.

What leverage really does

The headline "30:1 leverage" describes the maximum. What matters is your effective leverage: the size of your positions divided by your account equity.

In the example above, a £42,717 position on a £2,000 account is effective leverage of about 21:1. The arithmetic of that:

  • 0.50 lots on EUR/USD is $5 per pip, or about £3.94 per pip.
  • A 50-pip move against you — a perfectly ordinary day on EUR/USD — costs about £197, or 10% of the account.
  • A 100-pip move costs about £394, or 20%.

Now compare a sensibly sized trade on the same account. Suppose the chart says the stop belongs 30 pips away, and you decide to risk 1% of the account (£20) if it is hit. That works out at about 0.08 lots (the method is in Lesson 11): roughly £0.63 per pip, a notional value of about £6,835, and effective leverage of about 3.4:1. A 100-pip move against that position would cost £63 — but it never gets the chance, because the stop closes it at a £19 loss.

Leverage is often sold as "control a large position with a small deposit". The more honest description is: leverage multiplies the effect of every pip on your account, in both directions. It does not change the chart. It does not change your odds. It changes how hard each pip hits.

COMMON MISTAKE

Choosing position size by how much margin is available — "I have £2,000 and the broker lets me trade 0.70 lots, so I will". Available margin answers the question "how big can I go?". The only question that matters is "how much will I lose if my stop is hit?".

Margin calls and stop-outs

As an open position loses money, your equity (balance plus or minus open profit and loss) falls, while the margin used stays the same. The ratio between them is your margin level:

Margin level = equity ÷ margin used × 100%

Brokers act at set thresholds. Typically you get a margin call warning when the margin level falls to around 100%, and under UK and EU rules for retail clients, the broker must start closing your positions — a stop-out — when it falls to 50%.

Back to the over-leveraged 0.50-lot trade on £2,000, with £1,424 margin used:

  • Margin call at 100%: equity £1,424 → a loss of about £576 → about 146 pips against you.
  • Stop-out at 50%: equity £712 → a loss of about £1,288 → about 327 pips against you.

A 327-pip move in EUR/USD is not rare over a couple of weeks. And a stop-out does not close the position at a nice price; it closes it wherever the market is when the threshold is breached. You would lose around 64% of the account on one trade that never had a planned stop.

Negative balance protection and gaps

Under UK and EU rules, retail clients have negative balance protection: you cannot lose more than the money in your account. That is a safety net, not a strategy. Prices can gap — jump from one level to another without trading in between — over weekends and around big news. A gap can carry price straight through your stop, and your order fills at the next available price. Small, sensibly sized positions shrug gaps off. Over-leveraged ones do not.

Going deeper

Why regulators capped leverage. Retail leverage limits in the UK and EU (30:1 on major pairs, 20:1 on minor pairs and gold, lower on more volatile instruments) were introduced because retail losses on high-leverage products were persistently large. Some offshore brokers still offer 500:1 or more. Higher maximum leverage does not give you an edge; it gives you a bigger rope.

Leverage is an output, not an input. Professionals rarely think about leverage directly. They decide risk per trade (say 0.5–1%), find the stop on the chart, calculate the position size that makes the stop cost exactly that, and then check the resulting margin is comfortably affordable. Effective leverage drops out of that process — usually low single figures for a single trade. If you ever find yourself thinking "how much leverage should I use?", rephrase it to "how much am I prepared to lose if this is wrong?".

Correlated positions add up. Two trades that are both "short the dollar" — say long EUR/USD and long GBP/USD — behave much like one larger trade. Each may be sized at 1%, but a dollar rally can hit both stops together. For beginners, the simplest rule is one open trade at a time.

The maths of recovery. Losses are harder to recover than they look. Lose 10% and you need 11% to get back. Lose 20% and you need 25%. Lose 50% and you need 100%. Lose 64%, as in the stop-out example, and you need about 178%. Small fixed risk keeps you in the zone where recovery is realistic.

THE RULES
  • Every trade has a stop placed at the moment of entry; margin rules are never your stop
  • Position size is calculated from the stop and a fixed risk per trade, not from available margin
  • Keep margin used comfortably below half of your account equity
  • One open trade at a time while learning

Summary

  • Long profits from rising prices, short from falling; the stop always sits where the idea is proven wrong.
  • Margin is a deposit set aside to cover losses; at 30:1 it is about 3.33% of the position's value.
  • Effective leverage — position size divided by equity — is what decides how hard each pip hits your account.
  • Margin calls and stop-outs close over-leveraged trades at the worst moment; a planned stop and sensible size prevent both.
  • Your broker's leverage limit is not your risk limit. You set risk with your stop and your size.

quiz.q: You sell GBP/USD at 1.2700 and buy it back at 1.2640. What is the result?
options: Nothing — you cannot sell what you do not own
quiz.why: A short profits when price falls. Sold at 1.2700, bought back at 1.2640: 0.0060, which is 60 pips in your favour.

quiz.q: Where does the stop go on a short trade?
quiz.why: A short loses money when price rises, so the stop sits above entry at the level that proves the idea wrong.

quiz.q: A position has a notional value of £30,000 on a £3,000 account. What is the effective leverage?
quiz.why: Effective leverage = position size ÷ equity = £30,000 ÷ £3,000 = 10:1, regardless of the broker's maximum.

quiz.q: Equity is £900 and margin used is £1,200. What is the margin level, and what is likely happening?
options: 75% — below the margin call level, approaching stop-out
quiz.why: £900 ÷ £1,200 = 75%. That is below the typical 100% margin call level and heading towards the 50% retail stop-out.

quiz.q: Which statement about leverage is most accurate?
options: Higher leverage improves your chances of winning
Leverage multiplies how much each pip affects your account, in both directions
Leverage only matters on losing trades
Using maximum leverage is safer because positions close faster
quiz.why: Leverage does not change the chart or your odds. It changes the money attached to each pip — gains and losses alike.

quiz.q: In the 'Same chart, two very different accounts' example, why did the 0.08-lot trader lose only about 1%?
options: Because their broker gave them better prices
Because they had a stop placed at entry and a size calculated from it
quiz.why: The stop limited the loss to 30 pips, and the size was chosen so 30 pips cost about 1% of the account. The other trader had neither.

lessons.title: The Trading Sessions — When the Market Moves and When It Sleeps
lessons.summary: Identify the Asian, London and New York sessions in UK time, explain why price behaves differently in each, and choose trading hours that suit your pair, costs and life.
lessons.html:
Forex is open around the clock from Sunday evening to Friday night. That fact is usually sold as freedom: trade whenever you like. In practice it is closer to a trap. The market is open for 24 hours, but it is not equally alive for 24 hours. For long stretches it drifts sideways on thin volume and wider spreads. Then, at fairly predictable times, the big centres open, volume pours in, and the day's real moves happen.

A beginner who trades whenever they happen to be free will spend much of their time in the dead hours, paying more and seeing less. This lesson shows you the daily rhythm of the market so you can choose your hours deliberately.

All times below are UK time and approximate. Daylight saving changes on different dates in the UK, US and Australia, so the edges shift by an hour for a few weeks each spring and autumn. Your broker's server clock may also use a different time zone — check what your charts are showing.

The three main sessions

The trading day follows the sun round the world's financial centres.

Asian session — roughly 23:00 to 08:00. Sydney opens first, then Tokyo, Hong Kong and Singapore. Activity is concentrated in yen, Australian and New Zealand dollar pairs. On EUR/USD and GBP/USD, Asian hours are usually the quietest part of the day, with price often drifting in a narrow range.

London session — roughly 08:00 to 17:00. London is the world's largest forex centre. When it opens, volume jumps across every major pair, spreads tighten, and the day's first significant move often begins. The opening hour or two can be lively and occasionally violent as overnight orders are filled.

New York session — roughly 13:00 to 22:00. US banks and funds arrive, and major US economic data is typically released at 13:30 or 15:00 UK time. From around 17:00, once London closes, activity tends to fade through the evening.

The window when London and New York are both open — roughly 13:00 to 17:00 — is usually the most liquid of the day. For the dollar majors it is often where costs are lowest and moves are cleanest, though it also contains much of the day's scheduled news.

KEY POINT

The market is open 24 hours, but the bulk of the movement in the major pairs happens in a few hours around the London open and the London–New York overlap.

Why sessions behave differently

There is nothing magical about the clock. Price moves when large amounts of money need to change hands, and that happens when the institutions handling it are at their desks. During the Asian session, the banks that dominate euro and sterling trading are mostly asleep; liquidity in those pairs is thinner and there is less reason for big repricing. When London opens, a wave of corporate, fund and bank orders arrives at once.

Three practical patterns follow, all of them tendencies rather than rules.

The Asian range. EUR/USD and GBP/USD often spend the Asian session in a fairly tight band. The high and low of that band become reference points for the day.

The London open move. Early London often breaks out of the Asian range. Sometimes the first break is false and price reverses through the other side — which is why waiting for the first hour to settle can be wiser than reacting to the first candle.

The overlap and the data. Many of the most important US data releases land just as the overlap begins. Price can move sharply in either direction, then continue — or completely reverse — once the dust settles.

The dead zones

Just as important as knowing when to trade is knowing when not to.

  • Late New York into the roll-over (about 20:00 to 23:00). Volume fades, spreads widen around 22:00, and moves are often aimless.
  • The Asian session on European pairs. Low activity, and the tight range often means small moves relative to the costs.
  • Friday afternoon. Many participants square up positions before the weekend; moves can be erratic, and anything left open is exposed to a weekend gap.
  • Sunday evening open. Prices can open away from Friday's close, and spreads are often wide for the first hour.
  • Bank holidays in the UK or US, when one of the main centres is effectively shut.
COMMON MISTAKE

Trading the hours that fit your life rather than the hours that fit the market — typically late evening in the UK, the quietest and most expensive part of the day for EUR/USD and GBP/USD. If your free time falls there, use it for review and planning, not for live entries.

Choosing your hours

For most UK-based beginners trading the dollar majors, the sensible windows are:

  • 08:00 to 11:00 — the London morning, once the first 30–60 minutes have settled.
  • 13:00 to 16:00 — the overlap, avoiding the minutes either side of scheduled US data.

If you work during those hours, there are honest alternatives. You can trade higher timeframes (H4 and D1), where you place orders in the evening and let them work; the session matters less because each candle spans several sessions. Or you can choose pairs that are active when you are free — yen and Australian dollar pairs during Asian hours, for instance — accepting that you then need to learn their behaviour and costs.

What you should avoid is trading short-term setups on EUR/USD at 21:00 simply because that is when you are free. It is possible, but it is the hard way.

A simple session routine

Knowing the clock is only useful if it shapes what you actually do. Here is a routine that fits the London morning for a UK-based trader, and that you can shift to the overlap if that suits your day better.

  • 07:30. Open the economic calendar. Note any high-impact releases for the euro, the pound or the dollar today, and write down the 30-minute no-entry windows around them.
  • 07:45. Look at the H4 chart of your pair. Label the trend and mark the nearest zones (you will learn both in Lessons 8 and 9). Mark the Asian session's high and low.
  • 08:00 to 09:00. Watch, but do not act on the first move. Let the opening hour show you whether the Asian range is being broken cleanly or falsely.
  • 09:00 to 11:00. This is your active window. If price reaches one of your marked zones in line with the trend and gives you a trigger, you may trade it. If not, you do nothing.
  • 11:00. Stop looking for new entries. Manage anything open according to its plan, and write up the session in your journal — including the sessions where you did not trade.

The routine is short on purpose. Fixed hours protect you from the slow drift into trading whenever the screen is open, which is how most beginners end up trading the dead zones.

Going deeper

Liquidity and volatility are different things. Liquidity is how much can trade without moving price much; volatility is how far price actually moves. The London–New York overlap tends to be high in both. A news spike can be high volatility on low liquidity — dealers pull their prices, spreads widen and price jumps. That combination produces slippage.

Average range by hour. If you want evidence for your own pair, measure it: for the last few months, record the average high-to-low range of each hourly candle by time of day. The pattern is usually unmistakable. Compare that average range to your all-in cost. An hour whose average range is 6 pips with a 1.2-pip cost is a very different place to trade from one whose average range is 25 pips.

The economic calendar. Every serious broker and many free websites publish a calendar of scheduled data releases and central bank events, graded by expected impact. Check it at the start of each day. This course's simple rule for beginners is to have no new entries in the 30 minutes before and after a high-impact release on a currency in your pair, and to be wary of holding a trade with a tight stop through one.

Daylight saving. For a few weeks each March and October/November, the UK and US clocks change on different dates, so the overlap is an hour longer or shorter than usual and US data lands an hour earlier in UK time. Check, rather than assume.

THE RULES
  • Trade the London morning (after the first 30–60 minutes) or the London–New York overlap on the dollar majors
  • No new entries in the 30 minutes either side of high-impact scheduled news for either currency in the pair
  • No new short-term entries from 20:00 to 23:00 UK time or on Sunday evening
  • Check the economic calendar before the first trade of every day

Summary

  • The day runs through the Asian (about 23:00–08:00), London (08:00–17:00) and New York (13:00–22:00) sessions, UK time.
  • Most movement in the major pairs happens around the London open and the 13:00–17:00 overlap.
  • The Asian range is a useful reference; London often breaks it, and sometimes breaks it falsely first.
  • Late evening, Sunday open, Friday afternoon and holidays are low-quality, higher-cost hours.
  • Choose hours that suit the market; if your life does not fit them, trade a higher timeframe or a different pair.

quiz.q: Roughly when is the London–New York overlap in UK time?
quiz.why: New York opens around 13:00 UK time and London closes around 17:00, so both are active roughly 13:00–17:00 — usually the most liquid window of the day.

quiz.q: Why is EUR/USD often quiet during the Asian session?
options: Trading in EUR/USD is banned in Asia
The banks and funds that dominate euro and dollar flows are mostly not at their desks
Spreads are always zero in Asia
The euro is not traded on Mondays
quiz.why: Price moves when large flows need to change hands. During Asian hours, the main European and US participants are mostly inactive, so euro and sterling pairs tend to drift.

quiz.q: In 'The false start' chart, what happened after London broke above the Asian range?
options: The break failed and price fell through the bottom of the range
quiz.why: The upside break was rejected within an hour and price reversed through the Asian low. It illustrates why chasing the first opening candle is risky.

quiz.q: You hold a trade with a stop 15 pips away over the weekend, and the market opens 30 pips beyond your stop. What happens?
options: The stop fills at the stop level
The stop fills at or near the opening price, 15 pips worse
quiz.why: Price gapped through the stop without trading at it, so the stop becomes a market order and fills at the first available price — the gap price.

quiz.q: A beginner can only trade at 21:00–23:00 UK time and wants to trade EUR/USD on M5. What is the most sensible advice from this lesson?
options: Go ahead; the market is open
Use bigger size to make up for slow moves
Use that time for analysis and placing orders on higher timeframes, or trade a pair active at that hour
quiz.why: Late evening is quiet and costly for EUR/USD. Higher-timeframe orders or a pair active in those hours fit the market better than forcing short-term trades in dead hours.

lessons.title: Reading a Candlestick Chart — Bodies, Wicks and the Close
lessons.summary: Read any candle's open, high, low and close, tell momentum, indecision and rejection candles apart, and judge whether a candle pattern means anything by where it formed.
lessons.html:
Open any trading platform and the default chart is a row of little coloured bars with lines poking out of each end. Most beginners learn to say "green is up, red is down" and stop there. That is like learning to read by recognising the colour of the book covers.

Each of those bars is a candlestick, and each one is a compact summary of a fight between buyers and sellers over a fixed period of time. Learn to read that summary properly and a plain chart, with no indicators at all, starts telling you a great deal: who was in control, how hard the other side resisted, and whether that control is growing or fading.

This lesson teaches you to read single candles, then small groups of candles, and finally the most important idea in price action: a candle only means something because of where it formed. If you have watched the Trading Foundry film on why most traders cannot read charts, this is the longer, slower version.

Four prices, one picture

Every candle records four prices for its time period — one hour on an H1 chart, one day on a D1 chart:

  • Open — the first price of the period.
  • High — the highest price reached.
  • Low — the lowest price reached.
  • Close — the last price of the period.

The thick part, the body, spans the open and the close. If the close is above the open, the candle is bullish — drawn green here. If the close is below the open, it is bearish — drawn red. The thin lines above and below the body are the wicks (also called shadows). They show how far price travelled beyond the body before being pushed back.

KEY POINT

The body tells you the result; the wicks tell you the struggle.

The close is the verdict

Of the four prices, the close matters most. The open is where the argument started and the high and low are where it wandered; the close is where the period ended up — the price everyone holding a position was marked at when the candle finished.

This is why experienced traders wait for candles to close before reading them. Halfway through an hourly candle, GBP/USD might look like a huge bearish bar. By the close it might have recovered to leave a long lower wick — a candle that says nearly the opposite. Reading a candle before it closes is reading a match report at half-time.

One question will do more for your chart reading than any indicator: where did the candle close within its own range?

  • A close in the top quarter of the range: buyers finished in control.
  • A close mid-range: nobody won.
  • A close in the bottom quarter: sellers had the last word.

Three families of candle

There are dozens of named candle patterns. You need three families.

Momentum candles. Large bodies, small wicks, closing near the extreme. One side was in control for the whole period. Several momentum candles in a row in the same direction show a strong, committed move.

Indecision candles. Small bodies with wicks on both sides — the doji and the spinning top. Buyers and sellers fought to a draw. Indecision after a strong move often means the move is pausing; indecision in the middle of a choppy range means nothing much at all.

Rejection candles. A long wick on one side, a small body at the other end. The best-known is the pin bar: a wick at least twice the length of the body, with the body near one end of the range. A long lower wick says price was pushed down and then firmly rejected; a long upper wick says the reverse.

Location is everything

Here is the idea that separates candle reading from candle superstition. A candle pattern only means something at a meaningful price. A pin bar rejecting a level that has turned price several times before is evidence. The same pin bar floating in the middle of nowhere is just a candle with a long wick.

You will learn to mark those meaningful levels — support and resistance — properly in Lesson 9. For now, look at the difference.

COMMON MISTAKE

Memorising pattern names and trading every one that appears. Patterns found in empty space, against a strong trend, or in a tight sideways chop are mostly noise. Ask "where is this?" before you ask "what is this?".

Engulfing candles

One two-candle pattern is worth knowing now. A bearish engulfing pattern is a bullish candle followed by a larger bearish candle whose body completely covers the previous body. It shows buyers in apparent control being overwhelmed within a single period. A bullish engulfing is the mirror image. Like the pin bar, it carries far more weight at a level than in the middle of a range.

Reading candles in sequence

Single candles are words; a run of candles is a sentence. Most of the useful information on a chart comes from how candles change from one to the next, not from any one candle on its own.

Three sequences are worth learning to spot.

Expanding bodies. A run of candles in one direction, each with a bigger body than the last, shows the move gathering pace. Buyers (or sellers) are becoming more committed, and the other side is getting out of the way. Fading such a move — trading against it — is usually expensive.

Shrinking bodies. The same run, but with each body smaller than the last and wicks appearing on the side the move is heading towards. The move is still going, but each period gains less ground. This is often the first sign of a pause, especially when it happens as price approaches a level that has turned the market before.

Overlap. Candles whose bodies sit largely on top of each other, alternating colour, show a market going nowhere. Neither side can make progress. Signals inside heavy overlap are unreliable, because the chart has no direction for them to mean anything against.

A practical exercise: take any H1 chart, cover everything to the right of a candle with a piece of paper, and describe the last five candles in a sentence — "bodies getting smaller, wicks appearing above, approaching a previous high". Then slide the paper across one candle at a time. You are not trying to predict. You are training your eye to describe what is in front of it, which is the skill every later lesson depends on.

Going deeper

Every candle contains a chart. A daily candle is a summary of 24 hourly candles. A long lower wick on the daily chart is, on the hourly chart, a visible sell-off followed by a visible rally. The summary filters noise — but two very different days can print identical candles. That is one reason to read candles in sequence and in context rather than one at a time.

Higher timeframes carry more weight. A daily pin bar records the activity of a full day's participants. A one-minute pin bar might be a single order. The shapes look the same; the evidence is not. While you learn, read candles on H1 and above.

Candles are evidence, not prophecy. A rejection candle tells you what happened; it does not guarantee what happens next. Price action trading is the practice of stacking evidence — level, trend, candle, timing — until the odds lean slightly your way, and then limiting the damage when they do not. Even an A-grade pin bar at a strong level can and will fail. That is what stops are for.

Ranges and the body ratio. A useful objective test for momentum is body size as a fraction of the candle's total range. A body over about 70% of the range, closing near the extreme, is a momentum candle. A body under about 25% is indecision or rejection, depending on where the body sits. Measuring this keeps you honest when you "want" to see a pattern.

Summary

  • Each candle shows open, high, low and close; the body is the result, the wicks the struggle.
  • The close is the verdict. Wait for it, and ask where it sits within the range.
  • Three families: momentum (big bodies), indecision (small bodies, two-sided wicks) and rejection (long single wick, such as the pin bar).
  • Location decides meaning: patterns at support or resistance are evidence; in empty space they are mostly noise.
  • Engulfing candles show one side overwhelming the other; like all patterns, they matter most at a level.

quiz.q: A candle opens at 1.2700, trades up to 1.2735, down to 1.2690, and closes at 1.2730. What kind of candle is it?
quiz.why: The close (1.2730) is above the open, so it is bullish, and it is 5 pips from the high of a 45-pip range — in the top quarter. Buyers finished in control.

quiz.q: Which part of a candle shows where price was pushed but could not stay?
quiz.why: Wicks show the high and low reached beyond the body — prices that traded but were rejected by the close.

quiz.q: Why do experienced traders wait for a candle to close before acting on it?
options: Brokers do not allow trades mid-candle
The candle's shape can change completely before it closes
quiz.why: Until the close, a candle that looks strongly bearish can recover and leave a long lower wick — a very different message. The close is the verdict.

quiz.q: Compare the two pin bar charts. Why did one lead to a rally and the other mean nothing?
options: One was green and one was red
One formed at a support zone with history; the other formed in empty space in a downtrend
One was on a different pair
quiz.why: The shapes were nearly identical. Location made the difference: rejection at a level with history is evidence; the same shape in empty space is noise.

quiz.q: Which describes a bearish engulfing pattern?
options: A small bearish candle inside a large bullish one
A bullish candle followed by a larger bearish candle whose body covers the previous body
A bearish candle with a long lower wick
quiz.why: The second, bearish body completely covers the first, bullish body: buyers in apparent control were overwhelmed within one period.

quiz.q: A candle's body is 8 pips of a 40-pip range, with a 30-pip upper wick and the body at the bottom. What is it, most likely?
options: A bearish rejection candle (pin bar) — price was pushed up and rejected
quiz.why: A long upper wick, at least twice the body, with the body at the low end, shows a rally that was firmly rejected — a bearish pin bar. Whether it matters depends on where it formed.

lessons.title: Timeframes — Why Two Traders See Opposite Things
lessons.summary: Choose a sensible pair of timeframes, read the higher one for direction and the lower one for timing, and avoid the trap of trading against the bigger picture.
lessons.html:
Two traders look at EUR/USD at the same moment. One says it is clearly going up. The other says it is clearly going down. Both are looking at accurate charts from the same broker. Neither is wrong — they are simply looking at different timeframes.

This is one of the most common sources of confusion for new traders, and one of the most expensive. It produces the trader who sees a "downtrend" on the five-minute chart, sells, and is flattened by a daily uptrend they never looked at. It also produces the trader who flicks between six timeframes until one agrees with what they already wanted to do.

This lesson gives you a simple, fixed way to use timeframes: one for direction, one for timing, chosen in advance and never swapped mid-trade. It is the written version of the Trading Foundry film on timeframes.

What a timeframe is

A chart's timeframe is the period each candle covers:

  • M1, M5, M15 — one, five and fifteen minutes.
  • H1, H4 — one and four hours.
  • D1 — one day.
  • W1 — one week.

The market underneath is the same. A daily candle is simply the summary of 24 hourly candles; an hourly candle is the summary of 60 one-minute candles. Change the timeframe and you change the zoom, not the market.

But the zoom changes what you see. A strong daily uptrend contains plenty of hourly sell-offs. A neat-looking hourly downtrend may be nothing more than a two-day dip inside that bigger rise.

KEY POINT

Every timeframe is accurate. The question is not which one is true, but which one you let decide direction.

Higher timeframes carry more weight

Why should the higher timeframe usually win the argument? Because it summarises more trading. A daily trend reflects the decisions of every participant over weeks — including large funds and businesses whose orders take days to fill. A five-minute move might reflect a few large orders and some algorithms reacting to each other.

So when the hourly chart says "down" and the daily chart says "up", the most likely story is that you are looking at a dip in a rising market. It might become a reversal. But until the higher timeframe itself shows the trend breaking, the odds favour it continuing.

This leads to a simple discipline: use the higher timeframe for direction and the lower timeframe for timing. If the H4 chart is in an uptrend, you look only for buying opportunities on the H1 chart. If the H4 is in a downtrend, only selling opportunities. If the H4 is going sideways with no clear direction, you probably do nothing.

Pairing your timeframes

A common, workable rule of thumb is to use two timeframes roughly four to six times apart:

Direction (higher) Timing (lower) Typical holding time
W1 D1 Weeks
D1 H4 Days
H4 H1 Hours to a couple of days
H1 M15 Hours

For beginners, this course recommends H4 for direction and H1 for timing. It is slow enough to think, fast enough to see several opportunities a week, and the stops are wide enough that costs are a small fraction of them (Lesson 3). It also fits around most working lives better than you might expect: an H1 candle gives you an hour to decide.

The routine is called top-down analysis:

  1. On H4, decide the direction: uptrend, downtrend or no trend (Lesson 8).
  2. On H4, mark the key support and resistance zones (Lesson 9).
  3. Drop to H1 and wait for price to reach one of those zones in line with the H4 direction.
  4. Use an H1 candle signal at that zone as the trigger, with a stop beyond the zone.
COMMON MISTAKE

Timeframe shopping — flicking between charts until one tells you what you want to hear, or moving to a lower timeframe mid-trade to "check" a position and closing it on a five-minute wobble. Choose your two timeframes before you look at the market, and manage the trade on the timeframe you entered it on.

Why beginners should avoid the smallest timeframes

The one-minute and five-minute charts look exciting. Things happen constantly. That is precisely the problem.

On M1 and M5 charts:

  • The swings are small, so costs are a large share of every stop and target.
  • Noise dominates. Random wiggles are hard to tell from real moves.
  • Decisions have to be made in seconds, which favours emotion over thought.
  • You can take dozens of trades a day, which multiplies every mistake.

None of this makes short-term trading impossible — the Trading Foundry scalping course exists for those who want to learn it properly. It simply means it is the wrong place to learn.

A top-down routine in words

Here is what the routine sounds like in practice, on an illustrative Tuesday morning.

"On H4, EUR/USD has made three higher highs and three higher lows over the past two weeks. That is an uptrend, so today I am only interested in buying. The last swing high, broken yesterday, is at about 1.0900, and that area — 1.0892 to 1.0904 — is the nearest support zone below price. Price is currently 35 pips above it. Nothing to do yet."

Two hours later: "Price has pulled back into the zone. I switch to H1. The last H1 candle closed with a long lower wick and a body near its high, inside the zone. That is a rejection candle in the direction of the H4 trend, at an H4 level. Now I can plan a trade: entry above the candle's high, stop below the zone and the wick, target at least twice the risk and short of the next resistance."

Notice what did not happen. The trader did not look at the H1 chart until H4 had pointed somewhere. They did not take a trade because H1 looked exciting at 07:00. They did not check M5 to fine-tune anything. The higher timeframe made two decisions — direction and location — and the lower timeframe made one: timing. Keeping those jobs separate is most of the skill.

Going deeper

Fractal, but not identical. Markets look broadly similar at every zoom level — trends, pullbacks and ranges at every scale. But they are not identical. Lower timeframes have proportionally more noise and higher costs relative to the moves; higher timeframes have bigger stops, fewer trades and more exposure to overnight and weekend gaps. Pick the scale whose trade-offs suit your account, costs and time.

Alignment in three layers. Some traders add a third, higher timeframe for context — for example D1 for the big picture, H4 for direction and H1 for timing. When all three agree, the conditions are strongest. When the D1 is heading into a major resistance level, even a clean H4 uptrend deserves caution, because the bigger picture may be about to push back.

Candle times and your broker's clock. H4 and D1 candles open and close at times set by your broker's server clock. A broker on New York close time produces five daily candles a week; one on UK time may produce a small sixth candle on Sunday evening. This changes how daily candles look, so be aware which you are using if you compare charts.

Holding time follows timeframe. A trade entered on H1 with a stop based on H1 structure will usually take hours to a day or two to resolve. If you cannot leave a position open overnight, H1 entries late in the London afternoon may not suit you. Plan your timeframe around your actual availability.

THE RULES
  • Choose two timeframes before looking at the market: H4 for direction, H1 for timing in this course
  • Only trade in the direction of the higher timeframe's trend; if it has no clear direction, stand aside
  • Manage a trade on the timeframe you entered it on — no switching down to "check"
  • No M1 or M5 trading while learning

Summary

  • A timeframe is the period each candle covers; changing it changes the zoom, not the market.
  • Different timeframes can show opposite directions at the same moment, and both are accurate.
  • Higher timeframes summarise more trading and usually win the argument: use them for direction.
  • Use the lower timeframe for timing. This course uses H4 for direction and H1 for timing.
  • The smallest timeframes are dominated by noise and costs — the wrong place to learn.

quiz.q: The daily chart shows a strong uptrend; the hourly chart shows a run of lower highs and lower lows. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: The hourly chart is showing a pullback within the daily uptrend
Both charts are showing the same thing
quiz.why: Both are accurate. A smaller-scale decline inside a larger uptrend is a pullback. Until the higher timeframe itself breaks, the bigger trend is the stronger force.

quiz.q: Using this course's top-down approach, the H4 chart is in a downtrend. What should you look for on H1?
quiz.why: The higher timeframe sets direction. In an H4 downtrend you only look for H1 selling opportunities, typically as price rallies into resistance.

quiz.q: In 'Fighting the bigger trend', why was the short stopped out?
options: The stop was too far away
The H1 decline was a pullback in an H4 uptrend, and buyers resumed the bigger trend
The trade was entered on the wrong pair
quiz.why: The hourly pattern was real, but it was a dip inside a stronger four-hour uptrend. Trading against the higher timeframe put the trade on the weaker side.

quiz.q: Which is the biggest practical problem with M1 charts for a beginner?
options: Swings are small relative to costs and dominated by noise, and decisions must be made in seconds
Brokers charge more for M1 charts
They only work on yen pairs
quiz.why: Small swings make costs a large fraction of every trade, noise is hard to separate from signal, and the speed favours emotional decisions.

quiz.q: A trader enters on H1, then watches the M5 chart and closes the trade on a small five-minute drop that never threatened the H1 stop. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing; closing early is always safer
They switched timeframes mid-trade and let noise override the plan
They should have used a lower timeframe to enter
quiz.why: Manage a trade on the timeframe it was entered on. Dropping to M5 turns ordinary noise into a reason to abandon a plan that was still valid.

lessons.title: Trend or Range? Reading Market Structure
lessons.summary: Identify uptrends, downtrends and ranges from swing highs and lows, spot when a trend is breaking, and decide which conditions are worth trading at all.
lessons.html:
Before you ask "should I buy or sell?", there is a more important question: what kind of market is this? A market that is trending behaves very differently from one that is going sideways, and an approach that works well in one tends to lose steadily in the other. Most beginners never ask the question. They use the same idea everywhere and are baffled when it works for a month and then stops.

This lesson teaches you to read market structure — the pattern of swing highs and swing lows — so you can label any chart as an uptrend, a downtrend or a range, quickly and objectively. It is the foundation for the H4 "direction" step in the top-down routine from Lesson 7.

Swing highs and swing lows

Price never moves in straight lines. It moves in waves: a push, a pause or pullback, another push. The turning points of those waves are swings.

  • A swing high is a peak: a candle with lower highs on either side of it.
  • A swing low is a trough: a candle with higher lows on either side of it.

On any chart there are tiny swings everywhere. For reading structure, you want the obvious ones — the peaks and troughs you would point to if someone asked "where did price turn?". On H4, those are typically 30 to 100 pips apart on the major pairs. If you have to squint, it is not a swing.

The uptrend

An uptrend is a sequence of higher highs (HH) and higher lows (HL). Each push up goes further than the last, and each pullback stops above the previous pullback's low. Buyers are in control: they are willing to pay more on each wave, and they step in sooner on each dip.

The downtrend

A downtrend is the mirror image: lower highs (LH) and lower lows (LL). Each rally fails below the previous one and each sell-off breaks to a new low. Sellers are in control.

KEY POINT

Uptrend = higher highs and higher lows. Downtrend = lower highs and lower lows. Anything else is not a trend.

The range

A range is a market moving sideways between a reasonably clear ceiling and floor. Highs are roughly equal; lows are roughly equal. Neither side is in control for long. Markets spend a great deal of their time in ranges — often more than in trends.

In a range, the edges carry information and the middle carries very little. Buying in the middle has the ceiling as an obstacle a few dozen pips away and the floor as a stop a few dozen pips the other way — a poor trade-off either direction. For beginners, the simplest approach is: trade trends, and treat ranges as a reason to wait. Range-trading strategies exist and can be learned later, but they need their own rules.

When a trend ends

Trends do not last for ever. The structure itself usually gives the first warning.

In an uptrend, watch for two things:

  1. A failure to make a higher high. Price rallies but stalls below the previous peak. That is a lower high — the first crack.
  2. A break of the last higher low. Price falls below the most recent pullback low. Now the sequence of higher lows is broken too.

When both have happened, the uptrend is over as far as structure is concerned. That does not mean a downtrend has started — it may become a range — but it does mean you stop looking for buys.

COMMON MISTAKE

Calling the top of a trend on one big red candle. A single sharp drop inside an uptrend is usually just a pullback. Wait for structure — a lower high and a break of the last higher low — before deciding the trend has changed.

Practice drill: trend or not?

Here is a chart to read before you look at the answer. Label the structure, then decide: is this a market where a beginner using this course's approach should be looking for a trade?

Labelling structure, step by step

When you first try this, it can feel subjective. A simple, repeatable procedure helps.

  1. Open H4 with about two months of history. Remove indicators so you can see the swings.
  2. Mark the five or six most obvious turning points, working from left to right. Only mark swings where price clearly changed direction and travelled a meaningful distance afterwards — not every two-candle wobble.
  3. Compare each high with the previous high, and each low with the previous low. Write HH, LH, HL or LL next to each.
  4. Read the most recent three or four labels. HH and HL together: uptrend. LH and LL together: downtrend. A mixture, or roughly equal levels: range or transition.
  5. Write the verdict down — "H4: uptrend", "H4: downtrend" or "H4: no trend" — before you look at any other chart.

That last step matters more than it looks. If you write "no trend" and then catch yourself hunting for a buy on H1 an hour later, you have caught yourself breaking your own plan. Without the written verdict, you would never notice.

Ranges inside trends, trends inside ranges
