Structure exists on every timeframe at once, which is why Lesson 7 insists on one timeframe for direction. A healthy H4 uptrend often contains short H1 ranges — pauses where the market digests a move before the next push. Equally, a wide D1 range can contain perfectly tradeable H4 trends running from one side of it to the other.

This is not a contradiction. It simply means your label is always "an uptrend on H4" or "a range on H4". When the direction timeframe is trending, a small range on the timing timeframe is just a pause. When the direction timeframe is ranging, a neat trend on the timing timeframe is just a trip from one side of the box to the other, and it will probably stop at the far edge.

Going deeper

Choosing which swings count. Structure depends on which swings you treat as significant, and that is where subjectivity creeps in. Two practical aids: first, judge swings on your direction timeframe (H4 here), not on the timing timeframe. Second, a swing only "counts" if the move away from it was meaningful — for example, at least a third of the average daily range. Write your own definition down and apply it consistently; consistency matters more than which definition you pick.

Trend strength. Not all trends are equal. Strong trends have deep pushes and shallow pullbacks — a pullback that retraces only a third of the previous push. Weakening trends have shallower pushes and deeper pullbacks, often retracing more than two-thirds. Watching the ratio of push to pullback gives an early, objective clue that a trend is tiring before the structure actually breaks.

Moving averages as a helper. A moving average such as the 50-period EMA can help you see the trend at a glance: price mostly above a rising average in an uptrend, mostly below a falling one in a downtrend, and crossing back and forth through a flat average in a range. It is a summary of structure, not a replacement for reading it. The Trading Foundry trend courses go into this properly.

Regimes change. A market can trend for months and then range for months. Strategies that rely on trends tend to give back profit in ranges, and vice versa. Labelling the regime first, and having a rule for "no trade" conditions, is one of the simplest ways to avoid giving back what a good trend gave you.

THE RULES
  • Label the H4 structure before every trade: uptrend (HH + HL), downtrend (LH + LL), or range
  • Only look for buys in an H4 uptrend and sells in an H4 downtrend
  • A trend is over when it fails to make a new extreme and breaks its last pullback swing
  • In a range, or in the middle of one, stand aside

Summary

  • Structure is the pattern of swing highs and lows on your direction timeframe.
  • Uptrend: higher highs and higher lows. Downtrend: lower highs and lower lows. Range: roughly equal highs and lows.
  • In a range, the edges hold the information; the middle has none.
  • A trend ends when it fails to make a new extreme and then breaks its last pullback swing.
  • For beginners: trade trends, and treat ranges as a reason to wait.

quiz.q: Which sequence describes an uptrend?
quiz.why: Each peak higher than the last and each pullback low higher than the last: buyers are paying more on each wave and stepping in sooner on each dip.

quiz.q: In an uptrend, price rallies but stalls below the previous peak, then falls through the last higher low. What has happened?
quiz.why: A lower high followed by a break of the last higher low breaks the sequence. Stop looking for buys, even if a downtrend has not yet formed.

quiz.q: Why is the middle of a range a poor place to enter?
options: There is an obstacle on each side at similar distances, so neither direction offers a good stop-to-target trade-off
quiz.why: In the middle, a long faces the ceiling as an obstacle and a short faces the floor. The edges are where information and better trade-offs sit.

quiz.q: In the drill chart, what was the right decision?
options: No trade: it was a range and price was in the middle of it
Buy, because ranges always break upwards
quiz.why: The swings were roughly equal at top and bottom — a range — and price sat mid-range. A trend approach has no direction to follow; waiting is correct.

quiz.q: A downtrend makes a lower low, then rallies above the previous lower high. What does structure say?
options: The downtrend's sequence has broken; stop looking for sells until structure is clear again
Buy immediately; an uptrend is confirmed
quiz.why: Breaking above the last lower high breaks the LH/LL sequence. That ends the downtrend structurally, but one break does not yet prove an uptrend.

quiz.q: Which observation suggests a trend is weakening before its structure breaks?
options: Pushes getting longer and pullbacks shallower
Pushes getting shorter and pullbacks deeper
quiz.why: Shallower pushes and deeper pullbacks show the trending side is gaining less ground on each wave and the other side is fighting back harder.

lessons.title: Support and Resistance — Marking the Levels That Matter
lessons.summary: Draw support and resistance as zones rather than lines, grade a level's strength, recognise role reversal, and know when a level has failed.
lessons.html:
If you asked a room of experienced traders, using very different methods, to name one tool they all rely on, most would say the same thing: support and resistance. It is the oldest idea in charting and it is still the most useful. It tells you where price has turned before, and therefore where it is most likely to react again.

It is also one of the easiest tools to misuse. Beginners draw dozens of lines until the chart looks like a barcode, then any move can be "explained" after the fact. That is not analysis; it is decoration. This lesson teaches a stricter approach: few levels, drawn as zones, graded by evidence, and used only in the context of the trend you identified in Lesson 8.

What support and resistance are

Support is a price area where falling prices have repeatedly stopped and turned up. Buyers have stepped in there before.

Resistance is a price area where rising prices have repeatedly stopped and turned down. Sellers have stepped in there before.

Why would price remember a level at all? There are a few plausible, ordinary reasons. Traders who bought at a level and saw price rise are inclined to buy there again. Traders who missed the first move wait for a return to get in. Traders who bought just before a fall and endured a loss are inclined to sell when price comes back to their entry, to get out flat. Orders cluster around round numbers and obvious turning points. None of this needs a conspiracy; it is simply many people looking at the same chart and remembering the same prices.

KEY POINT

Support and resistance are areas where price has turned before. They are not magic; they are memory, and they tell you where a reaction is most likely.

Zones, not lines

Price is not precise. A level that turned the market three times did not turn it at exactly the same price each time: once the low was 1.0796, once 1.0802, once 1.0808. A single thin line forces you to pick one of those numbers, and price will spend its time poking through your line by a few pips and making you doubt it.

So draw zones: a band that covers the cluster of turning points. A useful starting rule on H4 is to draw the zone from the extreme wick to the area where the candle bodies turned. On the major pairs that usually gives a zone of roughly 10 to 25 pips. If your zone is 60 pips deep, it is not a level; it is a region, and you need a tighter definition.

How to draw your levels: a routine

Keep it simple and repeatable. On your direction timeframe (H4 in this course):

  1. Zoom out to show roughly two to three months of H4 candles.
  2. Find the obvious turning points — the swing highs and lows you would point to without hesitation.
  3. Look for clusters: places where two or more turning points line up horizontally.
  4. Draw a zone over each cluster, from the extreme wicks to where the bodies turned.
  5. Keep only the nearest two or three levels above price and the nearest two or three below. Delete the rest.

That last step matters. The levels that matter for your next trade are the ones price can reach in the next few days. A level 400 pips away is history, not information.

Grading a level

Not all levels are equal. Before you rely on one, grade it on a few simple questions:

  • How many times has it turned price? Two clean reactions is a level; three or more is a strong one.
  • How sharply did price leave? A strong move away shows real interest. A slow drift away shows little.
  • How visible is it? Levels obvious on H4 and D1 are watched by more people than those only visible on M15.
  • Is it a round number? Levels such as 1.1000 or 150.00 attract orders and attention.
  • Does it agree with the trend? In an uptrend, support zones where price might resume higher are the interesting ones. In a downtrend, resistance zones.

Role reversal: broken resistance becomes support

When price breaks decisively through a level, that level often changes role. Old resistance, once broken, tends to act as support when price comes back to it; old support, once broken, tends to act as resistance. Traders who sold at resistance and were proven wrong are keen to exit near their entry, and traders who missed the breakout get a second chance to buy.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating every level as a wall. Levels are areas where a reaction is more likely, not certain. Price breaks through levels all the time — which is why every trade at a level has a stop beyond it.

When a level fails

A level fails when price closes decisively through it and keeps going. On H4, a useful rule is: a candle body closing clearly beyond the zone, followed by a second candle that does not reclaim it. A wick poking through and snapping back is not a failure — that is often the level doing its job.

That losing trade is not a failure of the method. Levels fail, and that is exactly why the stop sits beyond the zone. But the chart did offer a warning: each rally from support was weaker than the one before, and the H4 structure was making lower highs. A support zone inside a market making lower highs is being leaned on, and buying it is buying against the structure.

Practice drill

A worked example of marking a chart

Suppose GBP/USD is trading at 1.2715 on H4, and you are preparing for the week. You zoom out to about ten weeks of candles and see:

  • three clear turning points between 1.2648 and 1.2660 over the past month, each followed by a rally of at least 60 pips;
  • two swing highs at 1.2788 and 1.2797, each followed by a sharp sell-off;
  • a former ceiling around 1.2700–1.2712 that price broke through a week ago and has not yet revisited;
  • assorted smaller wiggles everywhere else.

You draw three zones: 1.2648–1.2660 (support, three reactions — strong), 1.2700–1.2712 (old resistance, possible new support — untested since the break), and 1.2786–1.2800 (resistance, two reactions, near the round number 1.2800). You ignore the smaller wiggles.

Now you have a map. If the H4 trend is up, the interesting places for a buy are the 1.2700 zone (if price pulls back to it) and the 1.2650 zone below that. The obvious first target for any long is the 1.2790s. If price is sitting at 1.2715 right now, it is already just above the first zone — so the job is to wait, not to act. That is what most of good chart work looks like.

Going deeper

Levels as decision points, not predictions. Professional use of support and resistance is less "price will bounce here" and more "this is where I will find out who is in control". At a level, you have a nearby, logical place for a stop (just beyond the zone) and a clear test. That improves the geometry of a trade even if it does not change the odds very much.

Liquidity around obvious levels. Because many traders place stops just beyond obvious levels, price sometimes pokes through a level, triggers those stops, and then reverses. This is why stops placed right on the edge of a zone get hit so often, and why this course places stops beyond the zone and beyond the trigger candle's wick, with a small buffer for the spread.

Psychological levels. Round numbers (1.1000, 1.2500, 150.00) behave like levels even without prior history, because orders and option interest cluster there. Treat them as an extra reason a zone is important, not as levels to trade on their own.

Fewer levels, better levels. If you have more than about six zones on your H4 chart, you have too many. Every extra level is another excuse to see a trade that is not there.

THE RULES
  • Draw support and resistance as zones (typically 10–25 pips on H4 majors), not single lines
  • Keep only the nearest two or three zones above and below price
  • Only buy at support in an H4 uptrend and only sell at resistance in an H4 downtrend
  • Stops go beyond the zone and the trigger candle's wick, never inside the zone
  • A level has failed when an H4 body closes clearly beyond it and the next candle does not reclaim it

Summary

  • Support is where falling price has repeatedly turned up; resistance is where rising price has repeatedly turned down.
  • Draw zones over the cluster of reactions, not thin lines through one price.
  • Grade levels by number of reactions, strength of departure, visibility, round numbers and agreement with the trend.
  • Broken levels often change role: old resistance becomes support and vice versa.
  • Levels fail; a series of weakening bounces is a warning, and the stop beyond the zone is what limits the damage.

quiz.q: Why does this course draw support and resistance as zones rather than lines?
options: Price turns in clusters, not at one exact price; a zone covers the cluster and avoids false 'breaks'
Lines only work on yen pairs
quiz.why: Turning points differ by a few pips each time. A line forces you to pick one price and is pierced constantly; a zone covers the whole reaction area.

quiz.q: Price breaks above a resistance zone, rallies, then comes back to the zone. What often happens?
options: The zone often acts as support — role reversal
Price must fall back below it
quiz.why: Broken resistance often becomes support as trapped sellers exit and late buyers get a second chance. Often — not always.

quiz.q: Which observation best warns that a support zone may be about to fail?
options: Each bounce from support is weaker than the last, with lower highs
The zone is near a round number
The zone has been tested twice
A wick briefly pokes below the zone and closes back inside
quiz.why: Fading bounces and lower highs show sellers are gaining ground. A wick that snaps back inside is often the level working, not failing.

quiz.q: In the drill, why was buying at support the wrong call?
options: The zone had never held before
The H4 structure was a downtrend of lower highs, so a long was against the trend
Support zones can only be sold
quiz.why: The zone had held, but the highs were falling steadily. Buying support in a downtrend is buying against the structure — and the zone broke.

quiz.q: Where should a stop go on a long trade from a support zone?
options: In the middle of the zone
Exactly on the top edge of the zone
Beyond the bottom of the zone and the trigger candle's wick, with a small buffer
There is no need for a stop at strong support
quiz.why: If price closes beyond the zone the idea is wrong. The stop belongs beyond the zone and the wick, with a buffer for the spread, so normal probing does not trigger it.

quiz.q: You have drawn 14 zones on your H4 chart. What should you do?
options: Keep only the nearest two or three above and below price, based on the clearest reactions
Switch to M5 to see them better
quiz.why: Too many levels make every move 'explainable' and every trade look valid. The nearest few strong zones are the ones that matter for the next trade.

lessons.title: Order Types — Market, Limit, Stop, and the Orders That Protect You
lessons.summary: Choose between market, limit and stop orders for any entry, attach a stop-loss and take-profit to every trade, and understand when slippage and gaps can change your fill.
lessons.html:
You can have the best analysis in the world and still lose money on the mechanics. Beginners chase price with market orders at the worst moment, forget to attach a stop, or place a "stop" order thinking it is a "limit" and get filled in exactly the wrong direction. These are not trading mistakes so much as button mistakes. They are entirely avoidable.

This lesson covers the handful of order types you need, what each one does, and which to use when. It also covers the two orders that should accompany every single trade you ever place: the stop-loss and the take-profit.

Platforms name things slightly differently — "pending order", "entry order", "working order" — but the underlying types below are universal. Practise every one of them on a demo account before using them with real money.

Market orders: now, at the best available price

A market order buys or sells immediately at the best price available. Buy at market and you pay the current ask; sell at market and you receive the current bid.

Its strength is certainty of execution: you are in. Its weakness is uncertainty of price: in a fast market, the price you get may be worse than the price you saw when you clicked. That gap is slippage (Lesson 3).

Use market orders when your trigger has already happened and you want in now — for example, when an H1 signal candle has just closed and you are entering at the open of the next candle.

Limit orders: a better price, or nothing

A limit order waits for price to come to you, at a price better than the current one.

  • A buy limit sits below the current price. "Buy, but only if price falls to here."
  • A sell limit sits above the current price. "Sell, but only if price rises to here."

Limit orders fill at your price or better, so there is no negative slippage on entry. The cost is that the order may never fill — price can turn just before reaching it, and the move happens without you.

Stop orders: only if price proves the move

A stop order (as an entry, sometimes called a stop-entry or buy stop / sell stop) waits for price to move further in the direction you want, at a price worse than the current one.

  • A buy stop sits above the current price. "Buy, but only if price rises to here."
  • A sell stop sits below the current price. "Sell, but only if price falls to here."

Why pay a worse price? Because the stop order makes price prove itself first. If you want to buy only if price breaks above a candle's high, a buy stop just above that high does the job without you watching the screen. If price never gets there, you never get in — which is often exactly what you want.

KEY POINT

Limit = a better price than now (buy below, sell above). Stop = a worse price than now, as confirmation (buy above, sell below). Mixing them up enters you in the wrong direction at the wrong time.

The stop-loss: the order that keeps you in business

A stop-loss is an order attached to your open trade that closes it automatically if price reaches a set level against you. On a long trade it is a sell stop below entry; on a short, a buy stop above.

The stop-loss is not optional, not a sign of weakness and not something to "add later". It is the single order that turns an open-ended risk into a known one. This course's rule is absolute: the stop-loss is attached at the moment of entry, every time, at the level your analysis says the idea is wrong — beyond the zone and the signal candle's wick.

The take-profit: deciding the exit in advance

A take-profit is the mirror image: an order that closes the trade automatically when price reaches your target. A long trade's take-profit is a sell limit above entry; a short's is a buy limit below.

Placing it in advance has two benefits. You do not need to be watching when the target is reached. And you make the exit decision while calm, before greed and fear are involved.

When orders do not fill where you asked

A stop-loss is a stop order, and once triggered it becomes a market order. In normal conditions it fills at or very close to your level. In a fast market — a news release, a thin roll-over hour — or over a weekend gap, it can fill beyond your level.

That is not a reason to avoid stops. A stop that slips 6 pips is infinitely better than no stop at all. It is a reason to avoid holding small-stopped positions into scheduled news, and to keep position sizes modest enough that occasional slippage is survivable.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving the stop further away as price approaches it, "to give the trade more room". That converts a planned 1R loss into an unplanned bigger one, and it is the single most common way small losses become account-damaging ones. Stops move only in your favour, or not at all.

Which order for which job

Job Order Sits Fills
Enter now Market — Immediately, at best available price
Buy at a lower price Buy limit Below price At your price or better, if reached
Sell at a higher price Sell limit Above price At your price or better, if reached
Buy only on a break higher Buy stop Above price Once triggered, at next available price
Sell only on a break lower Sell stop Below price Once triggered, at next available price
Cap the loss Stop-loss Beyond your invalidation Once triggered, at next available price
Bank the target Take-profit At your target At your price or better

A worked example of all three orders together. EUR/USD is in an H4 uptrend and an H1 bullish pin bar has just closed at a support zone: high 1.0886, low 1.0871. The plan:

  • Entry: buy stop at 1.0888, two pips above the high. If price never trades above the pin bar, there is no trade.
  • Stop-loss: sell stop at 1.0868, below the zone and the wick, 20 pips from entry.
  • Take-profit: sell limit at 1.0928, 40 pips from entry — twice the risk.

All three are placed at the same time. Many platforms let you attach the stop-loss and take-profit to the pending entry order, so they activate automatically if it fills. Check that they have — a pending order with no attached stop is an accident waiting for a fast market.

Going deeper

Order duration. Pending orders have a time-in-force: "good till cancelled" (GTC) stays live until you remove it; "good for day" expires at the end of the trading day. Leaving a forgotten GTC buy stop live for a week is how traders discover they are in a trade they no longer want. Review pending orders every session.

OCO (one cancels other). Some platforms let you link two orders so that when one fills, the other is cancelled — for example, a buy stop above a range and a sell stop below it. Useful, but with a beginner's plan of one direction from the H4 trend, rarely necessary.

Trailing stops. A trailing stop follows price at a fixed distance as it moves in your favour, locking in profit. They sound ideal and often perform worse than expected in practice, because ordinary pullbacks hit them. Learn fixed stops and fixed targets first; experiment with trailing only once you have a journal to judge it against.

Entry choice changes results. A limit order at a zone gives a better price and a tighter stop but misses some trades; a stop order above a signal candle gets confirmation but a slightly worse price. Neither is right in general. This course's beginner plan uses a stop order above the signal candle, because confirmation keeps beginners out of trades where price never actually turns.

THE RULES
  • Every trade has a stop-loss and take-profit attached at the moment of entry
  • Stops move only in the trade's favour, or not at all
  • Enter with a buy stop above (or sell stop below) the closed signal candle, not by chasing with a market order
  • Cancel any pending order whose setup is no longer valid, and review pending orders every session
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Order type matches the plan: buy stop above / sell stop below the signal candle
  • Stop-loss attached beyond the zone and wick, plus spread
  • Take-profit attached at the planned target
  • No high-impact news for either currency within 30 minutes
  • Order duration set, and a reminder to review it

Summary

  • Market orders fill now at the best available price, with possible slippage.
  • Limit orders wait for a better price (buy below, sell above) and may not fill.
  • Stop orders wait for confirmation at a worse price (buy above, sell below).
  • Every trade carries a stop-loss and take-profit from the moment of entry.
  • Stops can slip in fast markets and gaps, which is a reason to avoid news with tight stops — never a reason to trade without one.

quiz.q: EUR/USD is at 1.0900. You want to buy only if it falls to 1.0870. Which order?
quiz.why: Buying below the current price is a better price than now, which is a limit order: a buy limit at 1.0870.

quiz.q: GBP/USD is at 1.2700. You want to buy only if it breaks above 1.2725. Which order?
quiz.why: Buying above the current price, as confirmation, is a stop order: a buy stop at 1.2725.

quiz.q: What type of order is the stop-loss on a short trade?
quiz.why: A short is closed by buying. The stop-loss buys if price rises to the level above entry, so it is a buy stop.

quiz.q: In 'A stop that slipped', why was the loss 1.5R instead of 1R?
options: A fast data-release candle jumped through the stop level and the fill came 6 pips worse
quiz.why: A triggered stop becomes a market order. In a violent news candle the next available price was 6 pips beyond the stop, turning a 12-pip loss into 18 pips.

quiz.q: Your long is 4 pips from its stop-loss. What does this course's rule say?
options: Move the stop further away to give it room
Leave it; stops move only in your favour or not at all
Double the position to average down
quiz.why: Widening a stop as price approaches it converts a planned loss into a larger unplanned one. Leave it alone.

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off between a limit entry and a stop entry?
options: Limit gets a better price but may miss trades; stop gets confirmation at a slightly worse price
Stop orders cannot be used for entries
quiz.why: A limit buys the price; a stop buys the confirmation. Each gives something up, and the plan should choose one deliberately.

lessons.title: Risk Per Trade and Position Sizing — The Maths That Keeps You Trading
lessons.summary: Choose a fixed risk per trade, calculate the exact position size for any stop on any pair in your own account currency, and measure results in R.
lessons.html:
If you take one lesson from this course into every trade you ever place, make it this one. Pattern reading, levels, timing — all of it matters, but none of it protects you if a single trade can do serious damage to your account. Position sizing is what makes losses small, equal and survivable. It turns trading from a series of bets into a process you can measure and improve.

The idea is simple: decide in advance how much of your account you are prepared to lose if a trade is wrong, put the stop where the chart says the idea is wrong, and then calculate the position size that makes those two numbers agree. The stop comes from analysis. The risk comes from your rules. The position size is the output — never the input.

This lesson works through the maths in full, with four worked examples in pound and dollar accounts. All exchange rates and figures are illustrative.

Step one: risk a fixed percentage

Professional and serious retail traders typically risk a small, fixed percentage of their account on each trade. For learning and early live trading, this course uses 0.5% to 1%.

On a £5,000 account:

  • 1% risk = £50 per trade.
  • 0.5% risk = £25 per trade.

Why a percentage rather than a fixed amount? Because it scales automatically. After a run of losses, 1% of a smaller account is a smaller amount, so you lose more slowly when things are going badly. After a run of wins, it grows with you. And it makes every trade the same size in risk terms, so no single trade can matter more than any other.

Why so small? Because losing streaks are normal. Even a sound method can produce long runs of consecutive losses over a few hundred trades. Look at what streaks do at different risk levels:

Risk per trade After 5 losses After 10 losses Gain needed to recover from 10
0.5% −2.5% −4.9% +5.1%
1% −4.9% −9.6% +10.6%
2% −9.6% −18.3% +22.4%
5% −22.6% −40.1% +67.0%

At 1%, ten losses in a row is an unpleasant fortnight. At 5%, it is a disaster that takes a 67% gain just to undo. The method is the same; only the size changed.

KEY POINT

Choose your risk per trade before you look at the chart, and keep it fixed: 0.5–1% of the account while you are learning.

Step two: put the stop where the chart says

The stop belongs where the trade idea is proven wrong — beyond the support or resistance zone and beyond the trigger candle's wick, plus a small buffer for the spread (Lessons 9 and 10). Measure the distance from entry to stop in pips.

You do not move the stop closer to allow a bigger position, or further away because a round number feels nicer. The chart decides the stop.

Step three: calculate the position size

The one formula:

Position size (lots) = money at risk ÷ (stop distance in pips × pip value per lot)

with the pip value per lot expressed in your account currency (Lesson 2).

Worked example 1: pound account, pound-quoted pair

  • Account £5,000, risk 1% = £50.
  • Pair EUR/GBP, stop 25 pips.
  • Pip value per lot: £10 (quote currency is GBP).
  • Size = £50 ÷ (25 × £10) = £50 ÷ £250 = 0.20 lots.
  • Check backwards: 0.20 × £10 = £2 per pip; × 25 pips = £50. Correct.

Worked example 2: pound account, dollar-quoted pair

  • Account £5,000, risk 1% = £50.
  • Pair GBP/USD, stop 25 pips. GBP/USD rate 1.2700.
  • Convert the risk into dollars: £50 × 1.27 = $63.50.
  • Pip value per lot: $10.
  • Size = $63.50 ÷ (25 × $10) = 0.254 → round down to 0.25 lots.
  • Check: 0.25 × $10 × 25 = $62.50 = £49.21. Just under £50 — the right side to miss on.

Worked example 3: pound account, yen pair

  • Account £5,000, risk 1% = £50.
  • Pair USD/JPY, stop 40 pips. GBP/JPY rate 190.50.
  • Pip value per lot: ¥1,000 ÷ 190.50 = £5.25.
  • Size = £50 ÷ (40 × £5.25) = £50 ÷ £210 = 0.238 → round down to 0.23 lots.
  • Check: 0.23 × £5.25 × 40 = £48.30.

Worked example 4: dollar account

  • Account $10,000, risk 0.5% = $50.
  • Pair EUR/USD, stop 20 pips. Pip value per lot $10.
  • Size = $50 ÷ (20 × $10) = 0.25 lots.

Notice the pattern in every example: round down, never up. Rounding up "because it's only a bit" is how 1% becomes 1.2%, then a habit.

The see-saw: stop distance and size

Here is the idea that clicks for most people once they see it. A wider stop does not mean "risking more". It means trading a smaller position, so the money at risk is unchanged.

COMMON MISTAKE

Tightening the stop to fit a position size you wanted to trade. That puts the stop where the money is comfortable rather than where the idea is wrong, and normal market noise then takes you out of trades that were never actually invalid.

Thinking in R

From now on, measure trades in R, where 1R is the amount you risked. Risked £50 and lost it: −1R. Made £100: +2R. Closed at break-even: 0R.

R makes every trade comparable, whatever the account size or pair, and it makes the most important relationship in trading easy to see. If your winners average 2R and your losers are 1R, the win rate you need just to break even (before costs) is:

Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + R)

  • Winners average 1R → need 50% winners.
  • Winners average 2R → need 33%.
  • Winners average 3R → need 25%.

This is why this course insists on a target of at least 2R. It gives the plan room to be wrong more often than it is right and still not lose money — before costs, and assuming every loss really is 1R.

That last assumption is where many traders fall down.

Going deeper

Expectancy. Over many trades, the average result per trade in R is:

Expectancy = (win rate × average win in R) − (loss rate × average loss in R)

As a purely hypothetical illustration: a plan that wins 40% of the time with average winners of 2R and losses of exactly 1R has expectancy (0.40 × 2) − (0.60 × 1) = +0.20R per trade. If sloppy stop management lets the average loss drift to 1.3R, the same entries give (0.40 × 2) − (0.60 × 1.3) = +0.02R — almost nothing. Most struggling traders lose their edge in the loss column, not the entry column. These numbers illustrate the arithmetic; they are not a claim about any strategy.

Costs in the sizing. Your real loss at the stop includes the spread and any commission. On tighter stops (under about 15 pips), add your typical all-in cost to the stop distance when sizing. On a 12-pip stop with a 1.2-pip cost, size for 13.2 pips.

Minimum size. If the calculated size rounds below your broker's minimum (often 0.01 lots), the correct answer is to skip the trade or find a setup with a tighter valid stop — never to take it oversized. On a very small account this binds often, and that is useful information: the account may be better used for practice at micro size than for live trading at "real" stakes.

One trade at a time, and a daily stop. Two trades on correlated pairs (EUR/USD and GBP/USD, for instance) can lose together, so 1% each is really closer to 2% on one idea. For beginners: one open trade at a time, and stop for the day after two losses. These are boundaries that protect your decision-making on bad days, when it is least reliable.

Practice drill

THE RULES
  • Risk a fixed 0.5–1% of the account per trade, chosen before looking at the chart
  • The stop goes where the chart says the idea is wrong; size is calculated from it, never the other way round
  • Round position size down, never up; if it rounds below the minimum, skip the trade
  • Never move a stop further away
  • One open trade at a time; stop for the day after two losses
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Risk amount in account currency written down (balance × risk %)
  • Stop distance measured in pips, including a buffer for the spread
  • Pip value per lot converted into account currency
  • Size calculated, rounded down, and checked backwards
  • Target at least 2R from entry

Summary

  • Risk a small, fixed percentage per trade (0.5–1% while learning); losing streaks are normal and size decides whether they hurt or harm.
  • Position size = money at risk ÷ (stop pips × pip value per lot), in your account currency, rounded down.
  • Wider stop, smaller size; tighter stop, larger size — the money at risk stays the same.
  • Measure trades in R. With 2R targets, you need about one win in three to break even before costs.
  • A moved stop destroys the arithmetic; planned losses must stay 1R.

quiz.q: Pound account of £8,000, risk 1%, EUR/GBP, stop 32 pips. What size?
quiz.why: Risk = £80. Pip value £10 per lot. Size = £80 ÷ (32 × £10) = £80 ÷ £320 = 0.25 lots.

quiz.q: Dollar account of $4,000, risk 0.5%, EUR/USD, stop 16 pips. What size?
quiz.why: Risk = $20. Size = $20 ÷ (16 × $10) = 0.125 lots. Round down to 0.12, never up.

quiz.q: Your stop on a trade widens from 20 to 40 pips. To keep the same risk, the position size should:
quiz.why: Risk = pips × pip value × size. Doubling the pips at the same risk means halving the size.

quiz.q: Your winners average 2R and losers 1R. Before costs, roughly what win rate breaks even?
In 'the moved stop', what did moving the stop do?
options: Turned a 1R loss into a 2.5R loss
Turned a loss into a win
Nothing, because the trade lost anyway
quiz.why: The planned 20-pip loss (−1R) became a 50-pip loss (−2.5R). One such trade cancels more than a full 2R winner.

quiz.q: In the £200 account drill, why was the right answer 'no trade' even though price rallied?
options: The setup was against the trend
The smallest available size risked about 1.6% of the account, breaking the 1% rule
The broker would not allow it
Support zones only work on D1
quiz.why: 0.01 lots × 40 pips ≈ £3.15, which is 1.6% of £200. The trade could not be sized within the rules. A good outcome does not make a rule-breaking decision correct.

lessons.title: Capstone — Building Your First Simple Trading Plan
lessons.summary: Assemble everything in this course into a written, one-page beginner plan; follow it through three fully worked trades, including a loss; and know exactly what to practise next.
lessons.html:
You now know what a pip is worth, what a trade costs, how leverage bites, when the market is awake, how to read candles, timeframes, trends and levels, which order to use, and how to size a position so that being wrong costs a fixed, small amount. Individually, those are pieces of knowledge. Put together and written down, they become a trading plan.

A plan is not a promise of profit. It is a set of decisions you make once, calmly, so that you do not have to make them again in the moment, when price is moving and your judgement is at its worst. It also makes your trading measurable: if you follow the same rules every time, your results tell you something about the rules. If you improvise, your results tell you nothing at all.

This capstone builds a deliberately simple beginner plan from the parts of this course, walks through three complete trades — two winners and a loser — and finishes with the one-page passport and the full pre-trade checklist. It is a training plan for learning on a demo account and then at the smallest live size. It is not a recommendation to trade anything in particular, and the example trades are illustrations, not real market history.

The eight parts of a plan

Every workable plan answers eight questions. Here are this course's answers.

  1. What do I trade, and when? One major pair — EUR/USD or GBP/USD — during the London morning (after the first 30–60 minutes) or the London–New York overlap. (Lessons 2 and 5.)
  2. Which timeframes? H4 for direction and levels; H1 for timing. (Lesson 7.)
  3. When is the market tradeable? Only when H4 shows a clear trend — higher highs and higher lows, or lower highs and lower lows. Ranges and unclear structure mean no trade. (Lesson 8.)
  4. Where do I look for entries? At an H4 support zone in an uptrend, or an H4 resistance zone in a downtrend, ideally one with role-reversal history. (Lesson 9.)
  5. What triggers the entry? A closed H1 rejection candle (pin bar) or engulfing candle out of the zone in the trend direction. Enter with a buy stop above its high, or a sell stop below its low. (Lessons 6 and 10.)
  6. Where is the stop? Beyond the zone and the signal candle's wick, plus a buffer of about the spread. (Lessons 9 and 10.)
  7. Where is the target, and how big is the trade? The next opposing swing or zone, and at least 2R away. Size so the stop costs 0.5–1% of the account. (Lesson 11.)
  8. What are my limits? One open trade at a time. Stop for the day after two losses. No entries within 30 minutes of high-impact news, or when the all-in cost is more than a fifth of the stop. Never move a stop further away. (Lessons 3, 4 and 11.)
KEY POINT

A plan is only useful if it is written down before you trade and followed exactly. An unwritten plan is a mood.

The playbook, step by step

Here is the plan as a routine you can run every session.

  1. Calendar check. Note any high-impact releases for EUR, GBP or USD today. Mark the 30-minute no-entry windows.
  2. H4 structure. Label the trend: up, down or none. If none, close the charts — there is no trade today on this pair.
  3. H4 zones. Mark the nearest two or three support and resistance zones above and below price.
  4. Wait. Set alerts at the zones in the trend's direction. Do nothing until price arrives.
  5. H1 trigger. When price reaches a zone, wait for an H1 candle to close. Is it a rejection or engulfing candle pointing with the trend? If not, keep waiting — or let the zone go.
  6. Measure. Entry (2 pips beyond the candle's extreme), stop (beyond zone and wick plus buffer), target (next opposing level). Is the target at least 2R? Is the cost under a fifth of the stop? If either answer is no, there is no trade.
  7. Size. Calculate the position for 0.5–1% risk, round down, check backwards.
  8. Place all three orders together: entry stop order, stop-loss, take-profit.
  9. Leave it alone. No moving the stop away, no early exits on lower timeframe noise.
  10. Journal. Screenshot before and after, the reasons, the R result, and one line on whether you followed the plan.

Worked trade 1: EUR/USD long (winner)

Account £5,000, risk 1% = £50. GBP/USD at an illustrative 1.2700.

H4 context. EUR/USD has made a clear series of higher highs and higher lows. The last swing high, around 1.0900, was broken strongly and price has now pulled back towards it. That old ceiling is the zone to watch: 1.0892–1.0904.

H1 trigger. Price reaches the zone during the London morning. An H1 bullish pin bar forms with a low at 1.0891 and a high at 1.0910, closing near its high. No news is due for two hours.

Measurements.

  • Entry: buy stop 2 pips above the high = 1.0912.
  • Stop: below the zone and the wick with a buffer = 1.0889. Distance 23 pips.
  • Next resistance: the prior high at about 1.0962. A 2R target is 46 pips → 1.0958, just below it. Target passes.
  • Cost: about 1.2 pips, around 5% of the stop. Passes.

Size. £50 × 1.27 = $63.50. Size = $63.50 ÷ (23 × $10) = 0.276 → 0.27 lots. Check: 0.27 × $10 × 23 = $62.10 ≈ £48.90.

Result: +2R. The trader did nothing between entry and exit, which is the point.

Worked trade 2: GBP/USD short (winner)

Same account and risk. H4 GBP/USD is in a downtrend: lower highs and lower lows. Price rallies into a resistance zone at 1.2740–1.2752 that was support before the last breakdown.

H1 trigger. A small bullish candle pokes into the zone, then a bearish engulfing candle closes at 1.2732, low 1.2730, high 1.2755.

Measurements.

  • Entry: sell stop 2 pips below the low = 1.2728.
  • Stop: above the zone and the high with a buffer = 1.2758. Distance 30 pips.
  • Next support: the prior low around 1.2660. A 2R target is 60 pips → 1.2668. Passes.

Size. $63.50 ÷ (30 × $10) = 0.212 → 0.21 lots. Check: 0.21 × $10 × 30 = $63.00 ≈ £49.61.

Result: +2R.

Worked trade 3: EUR/USD long (loser)

Same account and risk. H4 EUR/USD is in an uptrend and pulls back into a support zone at 1.0870–1.0882. Every box is ticked.

H1 trigger. A bullish pin bar: low 1.0871, high 1.0886, close 1.0884.

Measurements.

  • Entry: buy stop 1.0888. Stop 1.0868, 20 pips. Target 2R = 1.0928, just below the prior high at about 1.0934.
  • Size: $63.50 ÷ (20 × $10) = 0.3175 → 0.31 lots. Check: 0.31 × $10 × 20 = $62.00 ≈ £48.82.

Result: −1R. Across the three trades: +2R + 2R − 1R = +3R, about £148 on a £5,000 account. Do not read anything into that number — three trades are far too few to tell you anything about a plan, and you could just as easily show three losers in a row. The point of the example is the process: three trades sized identically, managed identically, with the loss kept at exactly the planned 1R.

COMMON MISTAKE

Judging a trade by its outcome. Trade 3 was a good trade that lost; a rule-breaking trade that happens to win is a bad trade. Judge decisions by whether you followed the plan, and judge the plan only over a large sample — at least 50 to 100 trades.

Practice drill: the target that is not there

The strategy passport

The whole beginner plan on one card:

  • Market: EUR/USD or GBP/USD. H4 for direction, H1 for timing. London morning or London–New York overlap.
  • Wait for: a clear H4 trend and price pulling back into an H4 support (uptrend) or resistance (downtrend) zone.
  • Trigger: a closed H1 pin bar or engulfing candle out of the zone in the trend direction; enter with a stop order 2 pips beyond it.
  • Stop: beyond the zone and the candle's wick, plus a spread buffer. Size for 0.5–1% risk.
  • Target: the next opposing level, at least 2R away. If the next obstacle is closer, there is no trade.
  • Avoid: ranges, unclear structure, high-impact news windows, wide spreads, more than one open trade, and anything you cannot size before clicking.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Economic calendar checked; no high-impact news for either currency within 30 minutes
  • Trading during the London morning (after the first 30–60 minutes) or the London–New York overlap
  • H4 structure labelled: clear uptrend or downtrend (not a range)
  • Price is in an H4 zone that agrees with the trend (support for longs, resistance for shorts)
  • A closed H1 pin bar or engulfing candle points with the trend
  • Entry stop order placed 2 pips beyond the signal candle
  • Stop beyond the zone and wick, plus spread buffer; distance measured in pips
  • Target at the next opposing level and at least 2R from entry
  • All-in cost under a fifth of the stop
  • Position size calculated for 0.5–1% risk, rounded down, checked backwards
  • No other trade open; fewer than two losses today
  • Entry, stop-loss and take-profit placed together
  • Journal entry started with a screenshot

How to practise this plan

  1. Backtest by hand. Scroll back through six to twelve months of H4 and H1 charts on one pair. Every time the checklist would have been met, record the trade in R. Be strict; record the losers honestly.
  2. Demo trade for at least 50 trades. Follow the plan exactly, in real time, with the position sizes you would actually use. Journal every trade.
  3. Review every 20 trades. Did you follow the plan? Where did you break it? What would the results have been if you had not?
  4. Only then go live, at the smallest size. Risk 0.5% or less at first. Your first live trades are about learning to follow the plan with real money at stake, not about income.

Going deeper

What this plan is, and is not. It is a sound learning framework that puts the core ideas of trend, location, trigger and risk into one routine. It is not a finished, tested strategy, and nothing in this course claims it will be profitable for you. The paid Trading Foundry courses exist to go deeper on each element: defining and filtering trends with moving averages, pullback depth and timing, support and resistance and supply and demand zones, candlestick price action, session-based day trading, and risk management in far more depth. The trend pullback course, in particular, is the natural next step from this plan.

Measure everything in R. Keep your journal in R-multiples. After 50 or 100 trades, calculate your win rate, average win, average loss and expectancy (Lesson 11). If average losses are larger than 1R, the problem is execution, not the setup. If you are taking trades outside the checklist, the problem is discipline. Both are fixable, and only a journal will tell you which you have.

Change one thing at a time. When you do start to refine the plan — a different trigger, a trailing exit, a third timeframe — change one rule, then trade at least another 30 to 50 trades before judging it. Changing several things at once leaves you unable to say what helped.

Expect the boring parts. Most sessions under this plan end with no trade. Most of the work is waiting at levels for candles that never form. That is not the plan failing; it is the plan filtering. Traders who cannot tolerate boredom tend to lower their standards until they are trading noise.

THE RULES
  • Follow the written plan exactly; any change is made between sessions, never during a trade
  • Trade only when every checklist item is met
  • 0.5–1% risk per trade, one trade at a time, stop for the day after two losses
  • Minimum 2R target, short of the next opposing level
  • At least 50 demo trades, journalled in R, before trading live at minimum size

Summary

  • A plan answers eight questions — what, when, timeframes, conditions, location, trigger, stop and target with size, and limits — and must be written down.
  • The playbook runs from calendar and H4 structure, through waiting at zones, to an H1 trigger, measurement, sizing and three orders placed together.
  • In the worked trades, two winners made +2R each and the loser cost exactly −1R; the process, not the result, is the lesson.
  • The drill shows the plan filtering a good-looking setup whose target was blocked by resistance.
  • Practise by hand-backtesting and demo trading for at least 50 trades before going live at minimum size.
